13.6.2.2 Local stresses at unstiffened junctions

Stress generation

The transfer of longitudinal force between a cylindrical section and a cone results in both a radial and an axial component at the junction, which generate:

a) local bending stresses in the tubular and the cone;   
b) hoop stresses in both the tubular and the cone.

Bending stresses

In lieu of a detailed analysis, the local bending stress at an unstiffened tubular-cone junction may be estimated from Formula (13.6-4):

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{j}} = 0. 85 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{j}}}{t}} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{t}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{t}}\right) \tan \alpha \tag{13.6-4}$$

where

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , j } }$ is the local bending stress at the junction;   
$D_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the outer diameter at the junction (see Figure 13.6-1);   
t is the wall thickness of the tubular member at the junction;   
σa,t $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } }$ is the axial stress in the tubular section at the junction due to global axial forces from factored actions;   
σb,t $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } }$ is the bending stress in the tubular section at the junction due to global bending moments from factored actions;   
α is the slope angle of the cone.

Hoop stresses

The hoop stresses at an unstiffened tubular-cone junction due to unbalanced radial line forces may be estimated using Formulae (13.6-6) and (13.6-7):

$$\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{t}} = 0. 45 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{j}}}{t}} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{t}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{t}}\right) \tan \alpha (13.6-6) \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{c}} = 0, 45 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{j}}}{t_{\mathrm{c}}}} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{t}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{t}}\right) \tan \alpha (13.6-7) \\ \end{array}$$

where, in addition to previous variables,

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , t } }$ is the hoop stress at the tubular side of the junction;   
$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , c } }$ is the hoop stress at the cone side of the junction.

At the smaller diameter junction, the hoop stress is tensile (or compressive) when $\left( \sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } } + \sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } } \right)$ is tensile (or compressive). Similarly, the hoop stress at the larger diameter junction is tensile (or compressive) when $\left( \sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } } + \sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } } \right)$ is compressive (or tensile); see Figure 13.6-2.

1 area of hoop compression

13.6.3 Strength requirements without external hydrostatic pressure

13.6.3.1 General

The properties of a conical transition shall be chosen to satisfy the requirements given in 13.6.3 and 13.6.4 for combined axial and bending stresses at each end of the cone and along the cone transition. Conical sections may generally be checked as tubular sections with equivalent diameters and actual thicknesses.

13.6.3.2 Local buckling within conical transition

For local buckling under combined axial compression and bending, the Formula (13.6-8) shall be satisfied at all sections within the cone:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{a , e q}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{y c}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c}}} \tag{13.6-8}$$

where

σa,eq $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , e q } }$ is the equivalent axial stress at any section s-s, see 13.6.2.1;

$f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ is the representative local buckling strength of a cone, in stress units;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , c } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial compressive strength (see 13.2.3.1).

For cones with slope angle $\alpha \leq 30^{ \circ } , f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ may be determined using Formulae (13.2-8) to (13.2-10),in which $f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength of the cone section being checked and t and D respectively are replaced by the wall thickness of the cone, $t_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ and an equivalent diameter, $D_{ \mathrm{ e } } ,$ both at the section under consideration. $D_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ is given by

$$D_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{D_{\mathrm{s}}}{\cos \alpha} \tag{13.6-9}$$

where $D_{ s }$ and α are defined in 13.6.2.1. If $\alpha > 30^{ \circ }$ , Formula (13.6-9) is not applicable.

The utilization of a cone, $U_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ under local buckling shall be calculated from Formula (13.6-10):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{c}} \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{a} , \mathrm{e q}}}{f_{\mathrm{y c}}} \tag{13.6-10}$$

13.6.3.3 Junction yielding

The requirements for junction yielding only apply to cases where the hoop stresses $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , t } }$ and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , c } }$ are tensile. Yielding at a junction shall be checked on both the tubular and the cone side of the junction using Formula (13.6-11) or Formula (13.6-12), as appropriate.

For net axial tension, i.e. when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is tensile:

$$\sqrt{\sigma_{\max}^{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}^{2} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\max}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t}}} \tag{13.6-11}$$

For net axial compression, i.e. when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is compressive:

$$\sqrt{\sigma_{\max }^{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}^{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} \left| \sigma_{\max } \right|} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t}}} \tag{13.6-12}$$

where

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is the maximum axial tensile stress at the junction;

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } } = \sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } } + \sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } }$ for checking yielding on the tubular side of the junction,

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } } = \frac{ \sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , c } } + \sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , c } } } { \cos \alpha }$ max for checking yielding on the cone side of the junction,

(see 13.6.2.1 and 13.6.2.2 for definitions of the stress components),

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the hoop stress at the junction

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } } = \sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , t } }$ for checking yielding on the tubular side of the junction;

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } } = \sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , c } }$ for checking yielding on the cone side of the junction;

$f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength of the tubular or cone section being checked;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , t } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial tensile strength (see 13.2.2).

The local bending stresses, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , j t } }$ and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , j c } }$ , at the junction shall be limited to the plastic moment capacities of the tubular member and conical transition wall thicknesses, respectively, in accordance with Formulae (13.6-12a) and (13.6-12b)

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{j t}} \leq 1. 5 \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t}}} \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\max} {}^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{y}} {}^{2}}\right) \quad \text{f o r c h e c k i n g o n t h e t u b u l a r s i d e o f t h e j u n c t i o n} \tag{13.6-12a}$$

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{j c}} \leq 1. 5 \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t}}} \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\max} {}^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{y}} {}^{2}}\right) \quad \text{f o r c h e c k i n g o n t h e c o n e s i d e o f t h e j u n c t i o n} \tag{13.6-12b}$$

The utilization of a junction of a conical transition, $U_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ for junction yielding shall be calculated from Formula (13.6-13) or Formula (13.6-14), as appropriate:

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{t}} \frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{\operatorname* {m a x}} {}^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\right)^{2} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} \cdot \sigma_{\operatorname* {m a x}}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} \quad \text{w h e n} \sigma_{\max } \text{i s t e n s i l e} \tag{13.6-13}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{t}} \frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{\max} {}^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\right)^{2} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} \cdot \left| \sigma_{\max} \right|}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} \quad \text{w h e n} \sigma_{\max} \text{i s c o m p r e s s i v e} \tag{13.6-14}$$

The utilization of a junction of a conical transition, $U_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ for local bending plastification shall be calculated from Formula (13.6-14a) or Formula (13.6-14b), as appropriate:

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{t}} \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{j t}}}{1 . 5 f_{\mathrm{y}} \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\max} {}^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{y}} {}^{2}}\right)} \quad \text{f o r c h e c k i n g o n t h e t u b u l a r s i d e o f t h e j u n c t i o n} \tag{13.6-14a}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{t}} \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{j c}}}{1 . 5 f_{\mathrm{y}} \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\max} {}^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{y}} {}^{2}}\right)} \quad \text{f o r c h e c k i n g o n t h e c o n e s i d e o f t h e j u n c t i o n} \tag{13.6-14b}$$

13.6.3.4 Junction buckling

The requirements for junction buckling only apply to cases where the hoop stress, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } } ,$ is compressive, and shall be checked on both the tubular and the cone side of the junction using Formula (13.6-15) or Formulae (13.6-19) and (13.6 20), as appropriate.

For net axial tension, i.e. when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is tensile, the following requirement shall be satisfied:

$$A^{2} + B^{2 \eta} + 2 \mathrm{v} A B \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.6-15}$$

where, in addition to the definitions given in 13.6.3.3,

$$A = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t}} \sigma_{\max }}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} \tag{13.6-16}$$

$$B = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{h}} \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}}} \tag{13.6-17}$$

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , h } }$ is the partial resistance factor for hoop buckling strength (see 13.2.6.2);

$f_{ \mathrm{ h } }$ is the representative hoop buckling strength, in stress units, calculated using Formulae (13.2-25) to (13.2-27), with $f_{ \mathrm{ h e } } = 0 , 4 E t / D_{ \mathrm{ i } } ;$

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the positive absolute value of the hoop compression;

ν is Poisson’s ratio, $\nu = 0 , 3 ;$

η is as defined in Formula (13.4-11);

The utilization of a junction of a conical transition, $U_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ for junction buckling when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is tensile shall be calculated from Formula (13.6-18):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = A^{2} + B^{2 \eta} + 2 v A B \tag{13.6-18}$$

For net axial compression, i.e. when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is compressive, the following requirements shall be satisfied:

$$\sigma_{\max } \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{y c}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c}}} \tag{13.6-19}$$

and

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{j}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{h}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{h}}} \tag{13.6-20}$$

where

$f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ is the representative local buckling strength of the section being checked, in stress units (see 13.2.3.3); for cones with slope angle $\alpha \leq 30^{ \circ } , f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ may be calculated in accordance with 13.6.3.2;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , c } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial compressive strength (see 13.2.3.1);

$f_{ \mathrm{ h } }$ is the representative hoop buckling strength, in stress units, calculated using Formulae (13.2-25) to (13.2-27), with $f_{ \mathrm{ h e } } = 0 , 4 E t / D_{ \mathrm{ j } } ;$

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the positive absolute value of the hoop compression.

The utilization of a junction of a conical transition, $U_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ for junction buckling when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ m a x } }$ is compressive shall be the larger value calculated from Formulae (13.6-21) and (13.6-22):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\sigma_{\max}}{f_{\mathrm{y c}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R , c}}} \tag{13.6-21}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R , h}}} \tag{13.6-22}$$

As in the case of junction yielding (see 13.6.3.3), plastification under local bending shall be checked using Formulae (13.6-14a) or (13.6-14b), as appropriate.

13.6.3.5 Junction fatigue

An unstiffened junction of a conical transition shall satisfy the fatigue requirements of Clause 16, with the following stress concentration factors, C:

$$C_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{j t}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{a} , \mathrm{t}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{t}}} \quad \text{o n t h e t u b u l a r s i d e} \tag{13.6-23}$$

and

$$C_{\mathrm{c}} = 1 + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{j c}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{a} , \mathrm{c}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{c}}} \quad \text{o n t h e c o n e s i d e} \tag{13.6-24}$$

where the variables are as defined in 13.6.2.1 and 13.6.2.2.1.

For equal tubular member and cone wall thicknesses, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , j t } }$ approximates to $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , j c } }$ and, similarly, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , c } }$ and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , c } }$ at the junction approximate to $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } }$ and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t^{ \prime } } }$ respectively, so that Formulae (13.6-23) and (13.6-24) reduce to:

$$C_{\mathrm{t}} = C_{\mathrm{c}} = 1 + 0, 6 \sqrt{\frac{2 D_{\mathrm{j}}}{t}} \tan \alpha \tag{13.6-25}$$

When using tapers at the ends of cones for connection to incoming tubulars, the taper should be on the inside of the small end of the cone and on the outside of the large end of the cone to keep stress concentration factors at a minimum.

13.6.4 Strength requirements with external hydrostatic pressure

13.6.4.1 Hoop buckling

Unstiffened conical transitions or cone segments between stiffening rings with a slope angle $\alpha \leq 30^{ \circ }$ , may be designed for hoop buckling as equivalent tubulars in accordance with 13.4. The equivalent diameter is $D / { \cos \alpha } ,$ where D is the diameter at the larger end of the cone or segment. An equivalent axial stress shall be used in the formulae in 13.4; the equivalent axial stress shall be calculated using Formula (13.6-1), substituting $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , c } }$ for $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t , c } } \ : 0 \ : \mathrm{ r } \ : \sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , c } } , \sigma_{ \mathrm{ t } } , \sigma \mathrm{ r } \ : \sigma_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ as appropriate. The length of the cone shall be taken as the maximum distance between adjacent rings for a ring-stiffened cone transition or the maximum unstiffened distance, including the tubular members on both ends of the cone, for an unstiffened conical transition. The tubular members on both ends of a ring-stiffened cone shall also be checked against the requirements of 13.4.

13.6.4.2 Junction yielding and buckling

The net hoop stress （$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } } )$ at a junction of a conical transition is given by Formula (13.6-26):

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{j}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{h}} \tag{13.6-26}$$

where

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the hoop stress at the junction due to unbalanced radial forces as defined in 13.6.2.2.3 and 13.6.3.3;   
$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h } }$ is the hoop stress due to forces from the factored external hydrostatic pressure (see 13.2.6).

When $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } }$ is tensile, Formulae (13.6-11) to (13.6-14) in 13.6.3.3 shall be satisfied using $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } }$ instead of $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ j } } .$ When $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } }$ is compressive, Formulae (13.6-15) to (13.6-22) in 13.6.3.4 shall be satisfied using $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } }$ instead of $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ { j } } } ,$ while the representative hoop buckling strength $f_{ \mathrm{ h } }$ shall be determined in accordance with 13.2.6.2 using the equivalent diameter as described in 13.6.3.2.

13.6.5 Ring design

13.6.5.1 General

A tubular-cone junction that does not satisfy the requirements of 13.6.3 or 13.6.4 can be strengthened either by increasing the tubular and cone thicknesses at the junction or by providing a stiffening ring at the junction. Where rings are provided, their dimensions shall satisfy Formulae (13.2-37) and (13.2-38) or Formula (13.2-39), as appropriate.

13.6.5.2 Junction rings without external hydrostatic pressure

If stiffening rings are required in the absence of hydrostatic pressure, their section properties shall satisfy both the following requirements:

$$A_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{t D_{\mathrm{j}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\right) \tan \alpha \tag{13.6-27}$$

$$I_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{t D_{\mathrm{j}} D_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}}{8 E} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\right) \tan \alpha \tag{13.6-28}$$

where

t is the thickness of the tubular member at the junction;   
$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a } }$ σa is the larger of $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } }$ (see 13.6.2.2.2) and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , c } }$ (see 13.6.2.1);   
σb $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b } }$ is the larger of $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } }$ (see 13.6.2.2.2) and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , c } }$ (see 13.6.2.1);   
$D_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the outer diameter at the junction (see Figure 13.6-1);   
$D_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ for external rings, is the diameter to centroid of composite ring section (see Figure 13.6-1);   
Dc $D_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ for internal rings, is taken as $D_{ \mathrm{ j } } ;$   
$\alpha$ is the slope angle of the conical transition, see Figure 13.6-1;   
$A_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the cross-sectional area of the composite ring section;   
$I_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the moment of inertia of the composite ring section.

In computing $A_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ and $I_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ the effective width of shell wall acting as a flange for the composite ring section (see Figure 13.6-1) may be computed from Formula (13.6-29):

$$b_{\mathrm{e}} = 0. 55 \left(\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{j}} t} + \sqrt{D_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{c}}}\right) \tag{13.6-29}$$

Where out-of-roundness is in excess of that permitted by Annex G, larger stiffeners can be required. The bending due to excess out-of-roundness shall be specifically investigated.

13.6.5.3 Junction rings with external hydrostatic pressure

If stiffening rings are required in the presence of external hydrostatic pressure, their section properties and spacing shall be chosen to satisfy Formulae (13.6-30), (13.6-31), (13.6-32) and (13.6-33):

$$\begin{array}{l} I_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{T}} \geq I_{\mathrm{c}} + I_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{h}} (13.6-30) \\ L_{1} \leq 1, 13 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{j}}^{3}}{t}} (13.6-31) \\ L_{\mathrm{c}} \leq 1, 13 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{e}}^{3}}{t}} (13.6-32) \\ \end{array}$$

where

$I_{ \mathrm{ c , T } }$ is the moment of inertia of the composite ring section in the presence of external hydrostatic pressure;   
$I_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the moment of inertia of the composite ring section in the absence of external hydrostatic pressure (see 13.6.5.2);   
$I_{ \mathrm{ c , h } }$ is the additional moment of inertia of the composite ring section required for external hydrostatic pressure

$$I_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{h}} = \frac{D_{\mathrm{c}} {}^{2}}{16 E} \left(t L_{1} f_{\mathrm{h e}} + \frac{t_{\mathrm{c}} L_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{h e c}}}{\cos^{2} \alpha}\right) \tag{13.6-33}$$

where

$D_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ Dc is as defined in 13.6.5.2;   
t is the wall thickness of the tubular member at the junction under consideration;   
$t_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the wall thickness of the cone at the junction under consideration;   
$\alpha$ is the slope angle of the conical transition (see Figure 13.6-1);   
$E$ is Young’s modulus of elasticity;   
$L_{ 1 }$ is the distance from the junction to the first stiffening ring in the tubular section (see Figure 13.6-1);   
$L_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the distance from the junction to the first stiffening ring in the cone, measured along the axis of the cone (see Figure 13.6-1);   
$f_{ \mathrm{ h e } }$ is the representative elastic critical hoop buckling stress of the tubular [see Formula (13.2-28)];   
$f_{ \mathrm{ h e c } }$ is the representative elastic critical hoop buckling stress of the conical transition treated as an equivalent tubular of diameter $D_{ \mathrm{ e } } { \mathrm{ , } }$   
$D_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ is the largest of the equivalent diameters for the bay of the conical transition adjacent to the junction under consideration [see Formula (13.6-9)].

The effective width of shell wall acting as a flange for the composite ring section (see Figure 13.6-1) may be computed from Formula (13.6-29).

A junction ring is not required for hydrostatic collapse if Formula (13.2-24) is satisfied using $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , j } }$ from 13.6.4.2. In satisfying Formula (13.2-24), the elastic hoop buckling stress, $f_{ \mathrm{ h e } } ,$ should be computed using Formula (13.2-28) with $C_{ \mathrm{ h } } = 0 { , } 44$ t cos $\alpha / D_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ .

Where out-of-roundness is in excess of that permitted by Annex G, larger stiffeners can be required. The bending due to excess out-of-roundness shall be specifically investigated.

13.6.5.4 Intermediate stiffening rings

If required, circumferential stiffening rings within conical transitions shall be designed using Formula (13.2-35) or Formula (13.2-36), as appropriate, with the following modifications:

— for internal rings, diameter D shall be taken as being equal to the equivalent diameter, $D_{ \mathrm{ e } } ,$ from Formula (13.6-9);   
— for external rings, diameter $D_{ \mathrm{ r } }$ shall be taken as being equal to the diameter, $D_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ to the centroid of the composite ring section, see Figure 13.6-1;-

— the wall thickness, $t ,$ shall be taken as being equal to the cone thickness, $t_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ at the position of the stiffening ring;   
— the spacing, $L_{ \mathrm{ r } } ,$ shall be taken as the average distance along the axis of the cone between adjacent rings;   
$- f_{ \mathrm{ h e } }$ shall be taken as the average of the representative elastic critical hoop buckling stresses for the two adjacent bays calculated using equivalent diameters, with the equivalent diameters based on the largest diameter for each of the adjacent bays.

## 13.7 Dented tubular members

13.7.1 General

Neither the effects of external hydrostatic pressure nor the presence of cracks have been considered in the derivation of the formulae of this subclause. Such effects shall be considered on a case-by-case basis. Fatigue problems can arise at dent locations and shall also be considered.

The limits of calibration for the formulae in this subclause are a dent depth, $h ,$ of $h \leq 0 , 3 \mathrm{ ~ D ~ }$ and $h \leq 10 t .$ The effects of dent depths in excess of either of these values shall be examined by other means.

13.7.2 Dented tubular members subjected to tension, compression, bending or shear

13.7.2.1 General

Dented tubular members subjected independently to axial tension, axial compression, bending or shear shall be assessed using the strength and stability requirements specified in 13.7.2.2 to 13.7.2.5.

13.7.2.2 Axial tension

Dented tubular members subjected to axial tensile forces shall satisfy the following condition:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{t}, \mathrm{d}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-1}$$

where

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t , d } }$ is the axial tensile stress due to forces from factored actions on the intact cross-section, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t , d } } = T / A_{ \mathrm{ r } } ;$

$T$ is the member axial tensile force;

$A_{ \mathrm{ r } }$ is the cross-sectional area of the intact section;

$f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength, in stress units;

$\boldsymbol{ \gamma }_{ \mathrm{ R , t , d } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial tensile strength for dented members, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , t , d } } = 1 , 05$

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under axial tension shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-2):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-2}$$

13.7.2.3 Axial compression

13.7.2.3.1 General

Dented tubular members subjected to axial compressive forces shall satisfy the following condition:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-3}$$

where

σc,d $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , d } }$ is the axial compressive stress due to forces from factored actions on the intact cross section, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , d } } = P / A_{ \mathrm{ r } } ;$

$P$ is the member axial compressive force;

$f_{ \mathrm{ c , d } }$ is the representative axial compressive strength of dented members, in stress units, see 13.7.2.3.2;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , c , d } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial compressive strength of dented members, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , c , d } } = 1 , 18 .$ .

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under axial compression shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-4):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-4}$$

13.7.2.3.2 Column buckling

The representative axial compressive strength for the dented members considered in 13.7.2.3.1 shall be determined from Formula (13.7-5) to Formula (13.7-15):

$$f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}} = f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}, \mathrm{o}} \quad \text{f o r} \Delta y / L \leq 0, 001 \tag{13.7-5}$$

$$\frac{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d} , \mathrm{o}}} + \frac{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} A_{\mathrm{d}} (\Delta y - 0 , 001 L)}{\left(1 - \frac{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{\xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{e} , \mathrm{d}}}\right) \xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}} Z_{\mathrm{e}}} = 1. 0 \quad \text{f o r} \Delta y / L > 0, 001 \tag{13.7-6}$$

where

$\varDelta y$ is the maximum out-of-straightness of the dented member;

$L$ is the unbraced member length, in the plane of buckling which coincides with the plane of $\varDelta y$

$f_{ \mathrm{ c , d } }$ is the representative axial compressive strength of dented members, in stress units;

$f_{ \mathrm{ c , d } , 0 }$ is the representative axial compressive strength of dented members when $\varDelta y / L \leq 0 , 001$ , in stress units

$$f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}, \mathrm{o}} = \left(1, 0 - 0, 278 \lambda_{\mathrm{d}}^{2}\right) \xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{y c}} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{d}} \leq 1, 34 \tag{13.7-7}$$

$$f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}, \mathrm{o}} = \frac{0 , 9}{\lambda_{\mathrm{d}}^{2}} \xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{y c}} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{d}} > 1, 34 \tag{13.7-8}$$

$f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ is the representative local buckling strength as defined in 13.2.3.3, in stress units;   
$f_{ \mathrm{ b } }$ is the representative bending strength as defined in 13.2.4, in stress units;   
$f_{ \mathrm{ e , d } }$ is the Euler buckling strength of the dented member, in stress units

$$f_{\mathrm{e}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\pi^{2} E}{\left(K_{\mathrm{d}} L / r_{\mathrm{d}}\right)^{2}} \tag{13.7-9}$$

$Z_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ is the elastic section modulus of the intact member as defined in 13.2.4;   
λd $\lambda_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the slenderness parameter of the dented member

$$\lambda_{\mathrm{d}} = \sqrt{\frac{f_{\mathrm{y c}}}{f_{\mathrm{e} , \mathrm{d}}}} = \frac{K_{\mathrm{d}} L}{\pi r_{\mathrm{d}}} \sqrt{\frac{f_{\mathrm{y c}}}{E}} \tag{13.7-10}$$

Kd $K_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the effective length factor of the dented member, which may be assumed to be the same as that for the intact member as defined in 13.2.3.2;

$r_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the radius of gyration of the dented member, which shall be calculated as

$$r_{\mathrm{d}} = \sqrt{\frac{I_{\mathrm{d}}}{A_{\mathrm{d}}}} \tag{13.7-11}$$

$I_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the effective moment of inertia of the dented cross-section

$$I_{\mathrm{d}} = \xi_{\mathrm{m}} I_{\mathrm{o}} \tag{13.7-12}$$

$I_{ \phantom{ }_{ 0 } }$ is the moment of inertia of the intact member, as defined in 13.2.3.2;

$A_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the effective cross-sectional area of the dented section

$$A_{\mathrm{d}} = \xi_{\mathrm{c}} A_{\mathrm{r}} \tag{13.7-13}$$

where

$A_{ \mathrm{ r } }$ is the cross-sectional area of the intact section, as defined in 13.2.3.2;

$\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ and $\xi_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ are coefficients defined by

$$\xi_{\mathrm{c}} = \mathrm{e}^{- 0, 08 h / t} \quad \text{f o r} h / t \leq 10, 0 \tag{13.7-14}$$

$$\xi_{\mathrm{m}} = \mathrm{e}^{- 0, 06 h / t} \quad \text{f o r} h / t \leq 10, 0 \tag{13.7-15}$$

h is the maximum depth of the dent, see Figure 13.7-1;

t is the thickness of the member.

13.7.2.4 Bending

13.7.2.4.1 General

Depending upon the plane of bending, dented cylindrical members subjected to bending can experience tensile, compressive, or zero (neutral) stress conditions existing in the central region of the dent (see Figure 13.7-1). Accordingly, they shall satisfy the requirements of 13.7.2.4.2 to 13.7.2.4.4.

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk1_0718334c4c6b7b0b4d679d3e9bdd94965863870b11cec519d7c718a9035174eb.jpg)  
Figure 13.7-1 — Sign convention for dented tubular

Key

1 dented section of the member   
$M^{ + }$ positive moment — dent in tension   
$M^{ - }$ negative moment — dent in compression   
$M^{ * }$ neutral moment — zero stress in centre of dent   
$h$ maximum depth of the dent

13.7.2.4.2 Positive bending

When the dented region is subjected to a positive bending moment $M^{ + }$ :

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{d}}^{+} = \frac{M^{+}}{Z_{\mathrm{e}}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{b}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-16}$$

where

$f_{ \mathrm{ b } }$ is the representative bending strength defined in 13.2.4, in stress units;

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ + }$ + is the positive bending stress due to forces from factored actions with respect to the intact crosssection, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ + } = M^{ + } / Z_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ ;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , b , d } }$ is the partial resistance factor for bending strength for dented members, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , b , d } } = 1 , 05$

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under positive bending shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-17):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}}{f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} = \frac{M^{+} / Z_{\mathrm{e}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-17}$$

13.7.2.4.3 Negative bending

When the dented region is subjected to a negative bending moment $M^{ - }$

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{M^{-}}{Z_{\mathrm{e}}} \leq \xi_{\mathrm{m}} \frac{f_{\mathrm{b}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-18}$$

where $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ - }$ is the negative bending stress due to forces from factored actions with respect to the intact cross-section, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ - } = M^{ - } / Z_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ .

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under negative bending shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-19):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{-}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} = \frac{M^{-} / Z_{\mathrm{e}}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-19}$$

where $\xi_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ is as defined in 13.7.2.3.2.

13.7.2.4.4 Neutral bending

When the dented region is subjected to a neutral bending moment $M^{ * }$

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{d}}^{*} = \frac{M^{*}}{Z_{\mathrm{e}}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{b}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-20}$$

where $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ * }$ is the neutral bending stress due to forces from factored actions with respect to the intact cross-section, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , d } }^{ * } = M^{ * } / Z_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ .

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under neutral bending shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-21):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} = \frac{M^{*} / Z^{\mathrm{e}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}} \tag{13.7-21}$$

13.7.2.5 Shear

Dented tubular members subjected to beam shear forces shall satisfy the condition specified in 13.2.5.1 in which the maximum shear stress due to forces from factored actions should be approximated by Formulae (13.7-22) and (13.7-23):

$$\tau_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{2 V}{A_{\mathrm{r}}} \quad \text{f o r} h \leq 0, 25 D \tag{13.7-22}$$

$$\tau_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{2 V / A_{\mathrm{r}}}{(1 , 5 - 2 h / D)} \quad \text{f o r} 0, 25 D <   h \leq 0, 3 D \tag{13.7-23}$$

where V and Ar are as defined in 13.2.5.1.

13.7.3 Dented tubular members subjected to combined forces

13.7.3.1 Axial tension and bending

13.7.3.1.1 General

Dented tubular members subjected to combined axial tension and bending forces shall satisfy the following conditions at all cross-sections along their length.

13.7.3.1.2 Axial tension, positive bending and neutral bending

Dented tubular members shall satisfy Formula (13.7-24):

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sqrt{\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}\right)^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}\right)^{2}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-24}$$

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ , under axial tension, positive bending and neutral bending shall be calculated using Formula (13.7-25):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sqrt{\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}\right)^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}\right)^{2}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \tag{13.7-25}$$

13.7.3.1.3 Axial tension, negative bending and neutral bending

Dented tubular members shall satisfy Formula (13.7-26):

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{-}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{\alpha} + \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-26}$$

where

$$\alpha = 2 - 3 \frac{h}{D} \tag{13.7-27}$$

and $\xi_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ is as defined in 13.7.2.3.2.

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ , under axial tension, negative bending and neutral bending shall be calculated from Formula (13.7-28):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{-}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{\alpha} + \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2}} \tag{13.7-28}$$

13.7.3.2 Axial compression and bending

13.7.3.2.1 General``, ``,

Dented tubular members subjected to combined axial compressive and bending forces shall satisfy the,``-`- following conditions at all sections along their length.``, ```,

13.7.3.2.2 Axial compression, positive bending and neutral bending

Dented tubular members shall satisfy Formulae (13.7-29) and (13.7-30):

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}}{\left(1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} / f_{\mathrm{e}}\right)}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} / f_{\mathrm{e}}}\right)^{2}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-29}$$

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sqrt{\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}\right)^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}\right)^{2}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-30}$$

where

$f_{ \mathrm{ y c , d } }$ is the representative local buckling strength of the dented member, in stress units;

$$f_{\mathrm{y c}, \mathrm{d}} = \xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{y c}} \tag{13.7-31}$$

$\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is as defined in 13.7.2.3.2;

$f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ is the representative local buckling strength of the intact member, as defined in 13.2.3.3;

$f_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ is the smaller of the Euler buckling strengths of the intact member in the positive and neutral bending directions, in stress units, as defined in 13.3.3.

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under axial compression, positive bending and neutral bending, shall be the larger value calculated from Formulae (13.7-32) and (13.7-33):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}}{\left(1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} / f_{\mathrm{e}}\right)}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{\left(1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} / f_{\mathrm{e}}\right)}\right)^{2} \right]^{0, 5} \tag{13.7-32}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sqrt{\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{+}\right)^{2} + \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}\right)^{2}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}} \tag{13.7-33}$$

13.7.3.2.3 Axial compression, negative bending and neutral bending

Dented tubular members shall satisfy Formulae (13.7-34) and (13.7-35):

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{\left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{\xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{e} , \mathrm{d}}}\right) \xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{\alpha} + \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{\left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{e}}}\right) f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-34}$$

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{-}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{\alpha} + \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{13.7-35}$$

where

$\alpha$ is as defined in 13.7.3.1.3;

$f_{ \mathrm{ e , d } }$ is as defined in 13.7.2.3.2;

$f_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ is the Euler buckling strength of the intact member in the neutral bending direction as defined in 13.3.3;

The utilization of a dented member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , d } } ,$ under axial compression, negative bending and neutral bending shall be the larger value calculated from Formulae (13.7-36) and (13.7-37):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \left\{\left[ \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \bar{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}}{\left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{\xi_{\mathrm{c}} f_{\mathrm{e} , \mathrm{d}}}\right) \xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}} \right]^{\alpha} + \left[ \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \bar{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}}{\left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{e}}}\right) f_{\mathrm{b}}} \right]^{2} \right\}^{0, 5} \tag{13.7-36}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{d}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{d}}}{f_{\mathrm{y c} , \mathrm{d}}} + \left[ \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{-}}{\xi_{\mathrm{m}} f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{\alpha} + \left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{d}}^{*}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2} \right]^{0, 5} \tag{13.7-37}$$

## 13.8 Corroded tubular members

The presence of local or overall corrosion should be taken into account in determining the residual strength of a corroded tubular member. There is insufficient information on the strength of corroded tubular members for inclusion of requirements in this document at time of publication. A methodology for estimating the effect of corrosion on member strength is discussed in A.13.8.

## 13.9 Grouted tubular members

13.9.1 General

This subclause applies to both fully grouted intact members and fully grouted dented tubular members, with the dent depth h limited to either $h { \le } 0 { , } 3 D$ or $h \leq 10 t$ . For grouted tubular members, neither the effect of external hydrostatic pressure nor the presence of cracks has been taken into account in the derivation of the formulae given in this subclause. Such effects shall be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Requirements for partially grouted tubular members are excluded, owing to the limited availability of relevant test data (see A.13.9.1 for additional information).

The strength model recognizes that grout filling inhibits the development of local buckling of intact tubulars and the growth of dents in damaged tubulars. Therefore, it is assumed that completely grouted tubular members can undergo column buckling, but not local buckling. However, in cases where local buckling can be important (e.g. large $D / t )$ , the representative steel yield strength, $f_{ \mathrm{ y } } ,$ may be replaced by the representative local buckling strength, $f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ (see 13.2.3.3).

13.9.2 Grouted tubular members subjected to tension, compression or bending

13.9.2.1 General

Grouted tubular members subjected independently to axial tension, axial compression or bending shall be assessed using the strength and stability requirements specified in 13.9.2.2 to 13.9.2.4.

13.9.2.2 Axial tension

Fully grouted tubular members subjected to axial tensile forces shall normally satisfy the following condition:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{t}, \mathrm{g}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{t}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t g}}} \tag{13.9-1}$$

where

σt,g $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t , g } }$ is the axial tensile stress in the steel tubular member due to forces from factored actions, neglecting the grout;

$f_{ \mathrm{ t } }$ is the representative axial tensile strength of the steel, in stress units, $f_{ \mathrm{ t } } = f_{ \mathrm{ y } } ;$

$f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength of the steel, in stress units;

$\boldsymbol{ \gamma }_{ \mathrm{ R , t , g } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial tensile strength of the grouted member, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , t , g } } = 1 , 05$

Where it can be demonstrated that complete grouting of the tubular has been achieved, $f_{ \mathrm{ t } }$ may be taken as $1 { , } 12 f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ .

The utilization of a grouted tubular member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , g } } ,$ under axial tension shall be calculated from Formula (13.9-2):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{t} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{t}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{t} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-2}$$

13.9.2.3 Axial compression

Fully grouted tubular members subjected to axial compressive forces shall satisfy the following condition:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{g}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-3}$$

where

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , g } }$ σc,g is the axial compressive stress in the fully grouted member due to forces from factored actions acting on the transformed area, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , g } } = P / A_{ \mathrm{ t r } }^{ }$ ;

$f_{ \mathrm{ c , g } }$ is the representative axial compressive strength of the grouted member, in stress units, as defined in Formulae (13.9-8) and (13.9-9);

$\boldsymbol{ \gamma }_{ \mathrm{ R , c , g } }$ is the partial resistance factor for axial compressive strength of the grouted member, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ { R , c , g } } } = 1 , 18 ;$

$P$ is the axial compressive force in the grouted member due to factored actions;

$A_{ \mathrm{ t r } }$ is the transformed area of the fully grouted member

$$A_{\mathrm{t r}} = A_{\mathrm{s}} + \frac{A_{\mathrm{g}}}{m} \tag{13.9-4}$$

$A_{ s }$ is the cross-sectional area of the steel

$$A_{\mathrm{s}} = (D - t) t \left[ \pi - \left(\alpha_{\mathrm{g}} - \sin \alpha_{\mathrm{g}}\right) \right] \tag{13.9-5}$$

$$\alpha_{\mathrm{g}} = \arccos  \left[ 1 - 2 h / (D - t) \right] \tag{13.9-6}$$

$A_{ \mathrm{ g } }$ is the cross-sectional area of the grout

$$A_{\mathrm{g}} = (D - 2 t)^{2} \left(\pi - \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} + 1 / 2 \sin 2 \alpha_{\mathrm{g}}\right) / 4 \tag{13.9-7}$$

$m$ is the ratio of elastic moduli of steel and grout, $m = E_{ \mathrm{ s } } / E_{ \mathrm{ g } } ( m = 18$ , in lieu of actual data);

$E_{ s }$ is Young's modulus of elasticity for steel;

$E_{ \mathrm{ g } }$ is the modulus of elasticity of grout;   
h is the maximum dent depth, if present;   
D is the outer diameter of the steel tubular member;   
t is the thickness of the steel.

NOTE The function arccos is the inverse of the function cos, i.e. $y { = } { \operatorname{ a r c c o s } { x } } \Longleftrightarrow x { = } \cos .$ y $0 \leq y \leq \pi$ .

The representative axial compressive strength of fully grouted tubular members is due to column buckling and shall be determined from Formula (13.9-8) to Formula (13.9-23):

$$f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{g}} = \left(1, 0 - 0, 278 \lambda_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}\right) f_{\mathrm{u g}} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{g}} \leq 1, 34 \tag{13.9-8}$$

$$f_{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{0 , 9}{\lambda_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}} f_{\mathrm{u g}} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{g}} > 1, 34 \tag{13.9-9}$$

$$\lambda_{\mathrm{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{f_{\mathrm{u g}}}{f_{\mathrm{e} , \mathrm{g}}}} \tag{13.9-10}$$

where, in addition to the definitions given above,

$\lambda_{ \mathrm{ g } }$ is the column slenderness parameter of the grouted member;

$f_{ \mathrm{ u g } }$ is the axial squash strength of the grouted member, in stress units

$$f_{\mathrm{u g}} = \left(A_{\mathrm{s}} f_{\mathrm{y}} + 0. 67 A_{\mathrm{g}} f_{\mathrm{c u}}\right) / A_{\mathrm{t r}} \tag{13.9-11}$$

$f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength of the steel, in stress units;

$f_{ \mathrm{ c u } }$ is the representative unconfined cube strength of grout, in stress units;

$f_{ \mathrm{ e , g } }$ is the Euler buckling strength of the fully grouted member, in stress units

$$f_{\mathrm{e}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\pi^{2} \left(E_{\mathrm{s}} I_{\mathrm{s}} + 0 . 8 E_{\mathrm{g}} I_{\mathrm{g}}\right)}{A_{\mathrm{t r}} \left(K L\right)^{2}} \tag{13.9-12}$$

K is the effective length factor (see 13.5);

L is the longer of the unbraced lengths in the y- and z-directions;

$I_{ s }$ is the effective moment of inertia of the steel cross-section

$$I_{\mathrm{s}} = \left[ (D - t)^{3} t \left(\pi - \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} - \frac{1}{2} \sin 2 \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} + 2 \sin \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} \cos^{2} \alpha_{\mathrm{g}}\right) / 8 \right] - A_{\mathrm{s}} e_{\mathrm{s}}^{2} \tag{13.9-13}$$

$I_{ \mathrm{ g } }$ is the effective moment of inertia of the grout cross-section

$$I_{\mathrm{g}} = \left[ (D - 2 t)^{4} \left(\pi - \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} + \frac{1}{4} \sin 4 \alpha_{\mathrm{g}}\right) / 64 \right] - A_{\mathrm{g}} e_{\mathrm{g}}^{2} \tag{13.9-14}$$

$$e_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{1}{2} (D - t)^{2} t \sin \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} \left(1 - \cos \alpha_{\mathrm{g}}\right) / A_{\mathrm{s}} \tag{13.9-15}$$

$$e_{\mathrm{g}} = (D - 2 t)^{3} \sin^{3} \alpha_{\mathrm{g}} / \left(12 A_{\mathrm{g}}\right) \tag{13.9-16}$$

The utilization of a grouted member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , g } } ,$ under axial compression shall be calculated from Formula (13.9-17):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-17}$$

13.9.2.4 Bending

Fully grouted tubular members subjected to bending forces shall satisfy the following condition:

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{M}{Z_{\mathrm{e}}} \leq \frac{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-18}$$

where, in addition to the definitions given in 13.2.4, 13.9.2.2 and 13.9.2.3,, `,,,

$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , g } }$ σb,``,,, ` is the bending stress due to forces from factored actions and, when $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , g } } > f_{ \mathrm{ b , g } } ,$ is to be considered as an equivalent elastic bending stress, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , g } } = M / Z_{ \mathrm{ e } } ;$ ;

M is the bending moment in the grouted member due to factored actions;

$f_{ \mathrm{ b , g } }$ is the representative bending strength of the grouted member, in stress units, defined as

$$f_{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{Z_{\mathrm{p}}}{Z_{\mathrm{e}}} f_{\mathrm{y}} \delta (1 + 0, 01 k) \tag{13.9-19}$$

$$\delta = 1 - 0, 5 \frac{h}{D} - 1, 6 \left(\frac{h}{D}\right)^{2} \tag{13.9-20}$$

$$k = 5, 5 \delta \left(\rho \frac{D}{t}\right)^{0, 66} \tag{13.9-21}$$

$$\rho = \frac{0 . 6 f_{\mathrm{c u}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}} \tag{13.9-22}$$

$Z_{ \mathrm{ e } } , Z_{ \mathrm{ p } }$ are calculated as in 13.2.4 for intact and ungrouted members;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , b , g } }$ is the partial resistance factor for the bending strength of grouted members, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , b , g } } = 1 , 05 ,$

The utilization of a grouted tubular member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , g } } ,$ under bending shall be calculated from Formula (13.9-23):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} = \frac{M / Z_{\mathrm{e}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} / \gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-23}$$

13.9.3 Grouted tubular members subjected to combined forces

13.9.3.1 Axial tension and bending

No requirements for fully grouted tubular members subjected to axial tension and bending forces are presented, because of the limited availability of relevant test data. Several approximate methods that can be used to estimate the interaction are discussed in A.13.9.3.1.

13.9.3.2 Axial compression and bending

Fully grouted tubular members subjected to combined axial compressive and bending forces shall satisfy the following conditions at all cross-sections along their length for intact tubulars, and along the dented section for damaged tubulars:

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} T_{1} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} + \frac{T_{2} \left(\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}\right)^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}^{2}} \leq 1, 0 \quad \text{f o r} \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} \geq \frac{K_{2}}{K_{1}} \tag{13.9-24}$$

$$\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} \leq 1, 0 \quad \text{f o r} \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} <   \frac{K_{2}}{K_{1}} \tag{13.9-25}$$

where, in addition to the definitions given in 13.9.2.3 and 13.9.2.4,

$$T_{1} = 1 - \frac{K_{2}}{K_{1}} - T_{2} \tag{13.9-26}$$

$$T_{2} = 4 \frac{K_{3}}{K_{1}} \tag{13.9-27}$$

$$K_{1} = 1, 0 - 0, 278 \lambda_{\mathrm{g}}^{2} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{g}} \leq 1, 34 \tag{13.9-28}$$

$$K_{1} = 0, 9 / \lambda_{\mathrm{g}}^{2} \quad \text{f o r} \lambda_{\mathrm{g}} > 1, 34 \tag{13.9-29}$$

$$K_{2} = \frac{K_{20} \left[ 115 - 30 (2 \beta - 1) (1 , 8 - \theta) - 100 \lambda_{\mathrm{g}} \right]}{50 (2 , 1 - \beta)} \quad \text{f o r} 0 \leq K_{2} \leq K_{20} \tag{13.9-30}$$

$$K_{3} = K_{30} + \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{g}} \left[ (0 , 5 \beta + 0 , 4) \left(\theta^{2} - 0 , 5\right) + 0 , 15 \right]}{1 + \lambda_{\mathrm{g}}^{3}} \tag{13.9-31}$$

$$K_{20} = \left(0, 9 \theta^{2} + 0, 2\right) \leq 0, 75 \tag{13.9-32}$$

$$K_{30} = (0, 04 - \theta / 15) \geq 0 \tag{13.9-33}$$

$$\theta = \frac{0 . 67 A_{\mathrm{g}} \left(f_{\mathrm{c u}} + \frac{C_{1} f_{\mathrm{y}} t}{D}\right)}{f_{\mathrm{u g}} A_{\mathrm{t r}}} \tag{13.9-34}$$

β is the ratio of the smaller to the larger end moment, with β = 1 if no end moments apply;

$$C_{1} = 4 \phi \varepsilon \left(1 + \phi + \phi^{2}\right)^{- 0, 5} \tag{13.9-35}$$

$$\phi = 0, 02 \left(25 - \frac{K L}{D}\right) \geq 0 \tag{13.9-36}$$

$$\varepsilon = 0, 25 \left(25 - \frac{K L}{D}\right) \geq 0 \tag{13.9-37}$$

The utilization of a grouted tubular member, $U_{ \mathrm{ m , g } } ,$ under axial compression and bending shall be the larger value calculated from Formulae (13.9-38) and (13.9-39):

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{c} , \mathrm{g}}} + \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} T_{1} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} + \frac{T_{2} \left(\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}\right)^{2}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}^{2}} \tag{13.9-38}$$

$$U_{\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{g}} = \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}} \sigma_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}}{f_{\mathrm{b} , \mathrm{g}}} \tag{13.9-39}$$

14 Strength of tubular joints

## 14.1 General

The requirements given in Clause 14 apply to the static design of tubular joints formed by the connection of two or more members. Members shall satisfy the requirements of 13.1 together with the additional requirements of 14.2.

Generic requirements for non-tubular joints are also given. Joint types are classified in 14.2.4.

In lieu of the requirements in this document, alternative methods may be used for the design of joints. Test data and analytical techniques may be used as a basis for design provided that it can be demonstrated that the strength of such joints can be determined reliably. Analytical or numerical techniques should always be calibrated and benchmarked to suitable test data.

The requirements have been derived from a consideration of the representative strength (as opposed to the mean strength) of tubular joints. Representative strength is comparable to lower bound strength. The background to, and a discussion of, the requirements are presented in A.14.

Care should be taken in using the results of very limited test programmes or analytical investigations to provide an estimate of joint strength, since very limited test programmes form an improper basis for determining representative values (see 7.7). In such cases, consideration shall be given to the imposition of a reduction factor on the calculation of joint strength to account for the small amount of data or for the inadequate number of calculations.

The nomenclature for simple joints is given in Figure 14.1-1. See also 12.3 and Figure 12.3-1. In all joint types, the chord is the through member. The chord where it forms the joint is usually referred to as a chord can or just can.

## 14.2 Design considerations

14.2.1 Materials

The provisions of this subclause apply to joints made of steels having representative yield strengths not exceeding 800 MPa. However, the usable value of yield strength as a fraction of ultimate tensile strength shall not exceed:

— 0,80 in the case of a chord;   
— 0,90 of the case of a brace.

Recommendations for grout materials for use in grouted joints are given in 19.7.

14.2.2 Design forces and joint flexibility

Joints shall be designed and assessed using internal forces resulting from factored actions in accordance with Clauses 8 to 11.

The reduction in secondary (deflection induced) bending moments due to joint flexibility or due to inelastic relaxation may be considered. For ultimate strength analysis of the structure, information on the force-deformation characteristics of joints may be used. These characteristics are dependent on the joint type, configuration, geometry, material properties, design situation under consideration and, in certain instances, hydrostatic pressure effects. See A.14.2.2 for a further discussion on joint flexibility.

14.2.3 Minimum joint strength

Chord cans, in addition to developing the strength required by design actions, shall have a minimum axial--`,,,` capacity of at least 50 % of the effective strength of each incoming brace for each design situation (in-,``,,, place, loadout, lifting, launch, accidental, etc.). `, `,,,

For earthquake actions, the chord can capacity shall be at least 100 % of the brace effective strength of ```,, each incoming brace for the in-place design situation.---

The effective strength of the brace is defined as the representative yield strength for braces where the axial component is tensile, Formula (13.2-1), or the compression buckling strength where the axial component is compressive, Formula (13.2-5) or Formula (13.2-6). The effective strength calculations shall be based on the nominal material and geometric properties of the brace, not those of the brace stub (if one exist).

For the purposes of this requirement, the chord can capacity shall be determined using the representative strength given in Formula (14.3-1). The strength factor $\left( Q_{ \mathrm{ u } } \right)$ and the chord force factor $\left( Q_{ \mathrm{ f } } \right)$ shall be consistent with the design situation being considered.

14.2.4 Weld strength

Welds in fabricated joints shall be designed to develop a strength greater than or equal to both the yield strength of the nominal brace cross-section (ignoring any brace stubs) and the full strength of the joint. Further guidelines for welds for circular tubular joints are given in Clause 20.

Joints often involve welds from several brace connections in close proximity. The high restraint of joints can cause large strain concentrations and a potential for cracking or lamellar tearing. Hence the chord material (and brace/stub material, if overlapping is present) shall have adequate through-thickness toughness, see Clause 19.

14.2.5 Joint classification

There are three basic planar joint types, Y-, K- and X-joints (also called cross-joints), as shown in Figure 14.2-1 and as described as follows:

a) A brace and a chord constitute a Y-joint if the component of the brace axial force perpendicular to the chord is reacted by beam shear in the chord. The brace axial force parallel to the chord is balanced by axial force in the chord.   
b) A pair of braces in the same plane and on the same side of a chord constitute a K-joint if the components of the brace axial forces perpendicular to the chord balance each other to within 10 %. The components of the axial brace forces parallel to the chord are balanced by an axial force in the chord.

c) A pair of braces in the same plane and on opposite sides of a chord or a brace in combination with other structural components on opposite sides of the chord (e.g. padeyes, launch rails) constitute a Xjoint if the axial force is transferred through the chord to the opposite side: there is no overall reaction in the chord.

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk1_8a2698c89c4ef9f6b92d9f7fff851793b12470829dd0821a9cf349695ecea15f.jpg)  
a) Y-joint

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk1_f126037cd0c37c2409a2c455bb61ca6ee9f16a990058f790ce6b19940df64c3d.jpg)  
b) K-joint

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk1_6477155f55b9dbd0bdeab5b2afed3f368edd78a1419a8c21fec4064a9f0d94d9.jpg)  
c) X-joint   
Figure 14.2-1 — Basic planar joint types

Fixed steel offshore structures are normally space frames containing mixtures of the above joint types either in one plane or in several planes (multi-planar joints). For the purposes of classification, all members in planes within ±15° of each other may be considered as being in one plane. Joint classification is based solely on consideration of the axial forces in the braces.

Variants of the above joint types are T-joints which are Y-joints where the angle between the brace and the chord is approximately 90° and DT-joints, or Double T-joints, which look like X-joints with angles of approximately 90°, but behave as two T-joints because the brace axial forces are transferred to the chord - rather than to the opposite brace.

The design strength of most joints can be determined using the parametric formulae given in 14.3 for the,,,`` three basic planar joint types. The practical use of the basic joint formulae shall reflect, as closely as,,,,`, possible, the force pattern assumed in deriving the formulae by classifying each combination of brace(s),,``,` and chord according to the flow of the axial force in the brace(s).

Classification shall apply to the combination of an individual brace with a chord (Y-joint) or combination of a pair of braces with a chord (K- or X-joints), rather than to the whole joint based on the axial force pattern for each design situation. Thus, an individual brace can form part of a K-joint and part of a Y-joint and shall be classified accordingly as a proportion of each relevant type, e.g. 50 % K-joint and 50 % Y-joint. This classification is relevant to both fatigue and strength considerations.

Classification shall proceed on the basis of assessing whether the joint is, firstly, a K-joint and secondly a Y-joint or a X-joint. Figure 14.2-2 shows some simple examples of the brace joint classification scheme.

Figure 14.2-2 h) is a good example of the axial force flow and classification hierarchy that should be adopted in the classification of braces in joints. The braces 1 and 2 on the left hand side of the chord act as a K-joint accounting for 50 % of the axial force in the diagonal brace. The other 50 % of the axial force in brace 1 forms an X-joint with brace 3. Replacement of brace axial forces by a combination of tension and compression forces to give the same net force is not permitted. For the example shown in Figure 14.2-2 h), replacing the axial force in brace 2 by a compression force of 1 000 and a tension force of 500 is not permitted, as this results in an inappropriate X-joint classification for this horizontal brace and a full K-joint classification for brace 1.

Careful consideration should be given to determining the correct gap between braces in a K-joint. In Figure 14.2-2 a) the appropriate gap is between adjacent braces. However, if an intermediate brace exists, as in Figure 14.2-2 d), the appropriate gap is between the outer braces acting as the K-joint. In this case, since the gap is often large, the K-joint strength can revert to that of a Y-joint. Figure 14.2-2 e) is instructive in that the appropriate gap for brace 2 is $g_{ 2 } ,$ , whereas for brace 1 it is $g_{ 1 } .$ . Although brace 3 is classified wholly as a K-joint (with brace 2 for 500 normal to the chord and with brace 1 for the remainder of the normal component of brace 3), the strength is determined by weighting the strength with gaps of $g_{ 1 }$ and $g_{ 2 }$ by the proportions of the axial force balancing from braces 1 and 2.

There are some instances where the above joint classification methodology is difficult to apply or is not applicable. Two of the more common cases in the latter category are associated with actions on a launch frame and with in situ actions on skirt pile-sleeves. Some guidance for such instances is given in A.14.2.5.

Once the classification is determined, joint strength can be determined using the procedures in 14.3.

14.2.6 Detailing practice

Joint detailing is an essential element of joint design. For unreinforced joints, the recommended detailing nomenclature and dimensioning are shown in Figures 14.2-3 and 14.2-4. Where an increased wall thickness or higher yield or toughness properties is required for the chord, this material should extend beyond the outside edge of incoming braces by the greater of a minimum of one quarter of the chord diameter, or 300 mm. The strength of Y- and X-joints is a function of the can length (see 14.3.5) and short can lengths can lead to a reduction in joint strength. Increasing the chord can lengths beyond the minimum values given here should be considered to avoid the need for downgrading strength.

In an X-joint, the larger diameter member shall continue through the joint, and the other should frame onto the through member. Where members of equal diameter meet at an X-joint, the member that carries the greater forces should be adopted as the through member.

When two or more braces intersect or overlap at a joint, the order in which each member frames into the joint should be determined by wall thickness and/or diameter. Typically the member with the thickest wall should be the continuous or through member, and the sequence for framing the remaining members should be based on the order of decreasing wall thickness. If two or more members have the same wall thickness, the larger diameter member shall be the continuous or through member. If two or more members have the same diameter and wall thickness, either member may be the through member unless the designer has designated a through member. Where substantial overlap occurs, the larger diameter brace should be specified as the through member. This through member can require an end stub to ensure that the thickness is equal to that of the overlapping brace. Lengths of brace welds which are covered by other brace connections shall be inspected by NDT prior to cover up.

When a brace requires increased wall thickness, higher yield strength, or more stringent toughness properties, such material should extend from its connection with the chord or beyond its connection with any overlapping brace(s) by the greater of the brace diameter or 600 mm.

Neither the chord can nor the brace stub minimum dimensions given above include the length over which any thickness taper occurs; any difference in thickness between chord can and chord member or between brace stub and brace member shall be tapered at 1:4 or lower, see Figure 14.2-3. For joints where fatigue considerations are important, tapering on the inside can have both an undesirable influence on crack origin and make early detection of cracks more difficult; for such joints, tapering should be on the outside (i.e. matching internal diameters).

The nominal gap (i.e. excluding weld toes) between adjacent braces, whether in-plane or out-of-plane, should not be less than 50 mm. Overlapping of welds of non-overlapping braces at the weld toes shall be avoided. When braces overlap, the overlap should be at least d/4 (where d is the diameter of the through brace) or 150 mm, whichever is greater. This dimension is measured along the axis of the through member, see Figure 14.2-3.

Longitudinal seam welds and circumferential welds should be located to minimize or eliminate their `,,,` impact on joint performance. The longitudinal seam weld of a brace should be located near the crown ``,,, heel of the joint, see Figure 14.2-3. The longitudinal seam weld of the chord should be separated from ,`,,,, incoming braces by at least 300 mm, see Figure 14.2-4. Where a chord requires a circumferential weld to-`-` achieve the desired can length, the weld should be positioned at a lightly loaded brace intersection, ```,,, between saddle and crown locations, see Figure 14.2-3.---

## 14.3 Simple tubular joints

14.3.1 General

Simple tubular joints are joints having no gussets, diaphragms, grout or stiffeners. Simple Y- and X-joints have no overlap of principal braces, but simple K-joints may have overlaps up to 0,6 D.

The validity ranges for the geometrical parameters, which are used in the formulae given in the remainder of 14.3, are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} 0, 2 \leq \beta \leq 1, 0 \\ 10 \leq \gamma \leq 50 \\ 30^{\circ} \leq \theta \leq 90^{\circ} \\ \tau \leq 1, 0 \\ \end{array}$$

For K-joints, the following validity range also applies:

$$- 0, 6 <   g / D$$

Annex A discusses approaches that can be adopted for joints which fall outside the above ranges.

14.3.2 Basic joint strength

The strength of a joint varies not only with its material properties and geometry, but also with the pattern of forces on each brace. Consequently, values of the strength can vary between design situations.

The strength of simple tubular joints should be calculated for each brace, for each individual force component of tension, compression, in-plane bending and out-of-plane bending, and for each design situation consisting of a combination of forces.

Representative strengths for simple tubular joints are given in Formulae (14.3-1) and (14.3-2):

$$P_{\mathrm{u j}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}} T^{2}}{\sin \theta} Q_{\mathrm{u}} Q_{\mathrm{f}} \tag{14.3-1}$$

$$M_{\mathrm{u j}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{y}} T^{2} d}{\sin \theta} Q_{\mathrm{u}} Q_{\mathrm{f}} \tag{14.3-2}$$

where

$P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ is the representative joint axial strength, in force units;

$M_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ is the representative joint bending moment strength, in moment units;

$f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ is the representative yield strength of the chord can (the lesser of SMYS or $^{ 0 , 8 }$ of the tensile strength), in stress units;

T is the chord wall thickness at the intersection with the brace;

d is the brace outside diameter;

θ is the included angle between brace and chord;

$Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ Qu is a strength factor (see 14.3.3);

$Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ is a chord force factor (see 14.3.4).

For braces with a mixed classification, $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ and $M_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ should be calculated by weighting the contributions from Y-, K- and X-joint behaviour by the proportions of that behaviour in the joint. This means that $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ and $M_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ can be different for each design situation considered, see A.14.3.2.

For X- and Y-joints with chord cans, $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ shall not exceed the strength limits defined in 14.3.5.

The design values of the strength of simple tubular joints are given Formula (14.3-3) and Formula (14.3- 4):

$$P_{\mathrm{d}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{u j}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{j}}} \tag{14.3-3}$$

$$M_{\mathrm{d}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{u j}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{R} , \mathrm{j}}} \tag{14.3-4}$$

where

$P_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the design value of the joint axial strength, in force units;

$M_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the design value of the joint bending moment strength, in moment units;

$\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , j } }$ is the partial resistance factor for tubular joints, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , j } } = 1 , 00$ .

In general, the strength factor, $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } } ,$ varies with joint classification and type of brace force: it is given in Table 14.3-1. For in-plane and out-of-plane bending, $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ is independent of joint classification.

14.3.4 Chord force factor, $\mathbf{ Q_{ f } }$

The chord force factor, $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } } ,$ is a factor that accounts for the presence of forces from factored actions in the chord:

$M_{ \mathrm{ p } }$ is the representative plastic moment strength of the chord can;

ipb refers to in-plane bending;

14.3.6 Strength check

Each brace in a joint that is subjected either to an axial force or a bending moment alone, or to an axial force combined with bending moments, shall satisfy:

$$U_{\mathrm{j}} = \left| \frac{P_{\mathrm{B}}}{P_{\mathrm{d}}} \right| + \left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{B}}}{M_{\mathrm{d}}}\right)_{\mathrm{i p b}}^{2} + \left| \frac{M_{\mathrm{B}}}{M_{\mathrm{d}}} \right|_{\mathrm{o p b}} \leq 1, 0 \tag{14.3-12}$$

where

$U_{ \mathrm{ j } }$ is the joint utilization;

PB $P_{ \mathrm{ { B } } }$ is the axial force in the brace from factored actions;

$M_{ \mathrm{ B } }$ is the bending moment in the brace from factored actions;

$P_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the design value of the joint axial strength (see 14.3.2);

$M_{ \mathrm{ d } }$ is the design value of the joint bending moment strength (see 14.3.2);

ipb represents in-plane bending;

opb represents out-of-plane bending.

## 14.4 Overlapping joints

The strength of joints with in-plane overlaps involving two or more braces (see 14.2.6) shall be determined using the requirements for simple joints defined in 14.3, with the following exceptions and additions:

a) Shearing of the brace parallel to the chord surface is a potential failure mode and shall be checked; see A.14.4.   
b) 14.3.5 shall not apply to overlapping joints.   
c) If axial forces in the overlapping and through braces have the same sign (both compression or both tension), when determining the strength of the through brace, $P_{ \mathrm{ { B } } }$ shall be calculated as the combined axial force equal to the force in the through brace plus a portion of the overlapping brace force(s). The portion of the overlapping brace force is calculated as the ratio of the cross-sectional area of the overlapping brace that bears onto the through brace to the full area of the overlapping brace multiplied by the force in the brace.   
d) When checking the strength of the through brace, the combined moments on the overlapping and through braces, taking account of the sign of the moments, shall be used to compute--`,,, $M_{ \mathrm{ B } }$ .   
e) The overlap onto the through brace shall be checked by using the through brace as the chord in the`,`,, formulae in 14.3. The through brace strength shall also be checked for combined axial force and`-`- bending moment in the overlapping brace in accordance with 14.3.6 using the value of,```,, $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ calculated for the through brace.`---   
f) Where nominal thicknesses of the overlapping and through braces differ by more than 10 %, the thicker brace shall be treated as the through brace. If this leads to β >1, β shall be taken as 1,0.

Joints having out-of-plane overlap can be checked on the same general basis as in-plane overlapping joints, except that the axial strength should normally revert to that for Y-joints.

## 14.5 Grouted joints

Two varieties of grouted joints are commonly used in practice. The first is a fully grouted chord, the second has a double-skin, whereby grout is placed in the annulus between an outer chord and an internal member. In both cases, the grout is unreinforced and no benefit to joint strength shall be derived from shear keys (if present).

The strength of grouted joints that are otherwise of simple configuration may be determined using the simple joint requirements defined in 14.3, with the modifications and limitations below.

a) For double-skin grouted joints, an effective thickness, $T_{ \mathrm{ e } , }$ should be determined from Formula (14.5-1):

$$T_{\mathrm{e}} = \left(T^{2} + T_{\mathrm{p}}^{2}\right)^{0, 5} \tag{14.5-1}$$

where

$T$ is the wall thickness of the chord;

$T_{ \mathbf{ p } }$ is the wall thickness of the inner member.

The effective thickness, $T_{ \mathrm{ e } } ,$ should be used in place of T in the simple joint equations, including the determination of the γ parameter, but taking into account b) and c) hereafter.

b) The $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ values given in Table 14.3-1 should be replaced with values pertinent to grouted joints determined from Table A.14.5-1. As the expressions in Table A.14.5-1 are based on tear-out of the chord wall, the chord wall thickness, T, should be used instead of the effective thickness, $T_{ \mathrm{ e } } . Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ values should not be less than those for simple ungrouted joints with the same geometry and forces. The reduction in the strength of Y- and X-joints due to length effects (see 14.3.5) may be disregarded for fully grouted joints, but should be included for double-skin grouted joints.   
c) The $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ value calculated from Formulae (14.3-9) and (14.3-10) depends on joint type and brace loading through the coefficients in Table 14.3-2, but not on thickness.   
d) Axial and moment design strengths calculated for the joint shall exceed the brace design strengths, for non-compact members inclusive of the local buckling strength at the brace end.

## 14.6 Ring stiffened joints

Primary joints along launch frames are often strengthened by ring stiffening. Ring stiffening is also used in some structures to address fatigue requirements or to avoid very thick chord cans. A.14.6 outlines the salient features of several common approaches available to design ring-stiffened joints.

## 14.7 Other joint types

Joints not covered by 14.3 to 14.6 may be designed on the basis of appropriate experimental, numerical, or in-service evidence.

For circular joints with doubler or collar plates, material strength approaches may be employed, although extreme care is needed in identifying all components that are expected to participate in resisting incoming brace forces and in establishing the acting force envelopes prior to conducting strength checks. Often material strength checks are complemented with calibrated FEA to establish the magnitude and location of acting stresses.

## 14.8 Damaged joints

Joints in existing structures can become damaged as a result of fatigue, corrosion, or overload (environmental or accidental). In such cases, the reduced joint strength shall be estimated from simple

models, e.g. based on the use of reduced area or section modulus, from more extensive numerical analysis using FEA models, or from experimental evidence.

## 14.9 Non-circular joints

Joints with non-circular chord or brace sections are typically used in topsides structures, see ISO 19901-3. Common types include I beam, column, and plate girder sections and rectangular or square hollow sections. For some configurations, detailed land-based design practice is available, see A.14.9. For arrangements for which little or no practice is available, the requirements are similar to those according to 14.7.

## 14.10 Cast joints

Cast joints can be of any geometry and are usually of variable wall thickness; they are of particular benefit when there are many similar joints or where fatigue is causing difficulties. The design of a cast joint requires calibrated FEA. A conservative design approach for strength is to limit stresses in the joint due to forces from factored actions to below the design yield strength of the material, $f_{ \mathrm{ y } } / \gamma_{ \mathrm{ R , q } }$ (see 14.3.4). The design of cast joints is often carried out in conjunction with the manufacturer.

15 Strength and fatigue resistance of other structural components

## 15.1 Grouted connections

15.1.1 General

Forces can be transferred between concentric tubular members by grouting the annulus between them. These forces are transferred from steel member to steel member, across the steel to grout interfaces and through the grout. Such connections are most commonly used for foundation pile-to-sleeve connections, but are also used for other types of connections, such as connecting pins and repairs.

The grout shall comply with the requirements of 19.7. Fabrication and installation shall be in accordance with 20.4.5 and 22.5.12, respectively.

In lieu of the requirements in this document, alternative methods may be used for the design of grouted connections. Test data and analytical techniques may be used as a basis for design provided that it can be demonstrated that the strength of such joints can be determined reliably. Analytical or numerical techniques should always be calibrated and benchmarked to suitable test data.

Within 15.1, the nomenclature and symbols shown in Figure 15.1-1 and Figure 15.1-2 are used.

15.1.2 Detailing requirements
