## A.13.3.4 Axial tension or compression, bending, shear and torsion

The value of torsion that can be ignored when coexisting with axial tension or compression, bending and shear, of 20 % of the representative shear yield strength, is based on a similar requirement in Reference [A.13.3-5]. The formula to determine the reduced representative yield strength for values of torsion in excess of 20 % is based on that prescribed in Reference [A.13.2-22].

The effect of shear on tubular member strength is based on the approach documented in Reference [A.13.2-22]. This assumes shear and shear yielding are limited in their extent to the shear area prescribed by Formula (13.2-16), i.e. half the cross-sectional area. Over the shear area, yielding is controlled by the Mises-Hencky criterion. Over the remaining area, direct stresses up to yield are permitted whether bending stresses or axial stresses. Reference [A.13.2-22] states that the effect of shear on bending and axial behaviour can be ignored for levels of shear up to half the representative shear strength. Formulae (13.3-13), (13.3-15) and (13.3-17) prescribe the form of interaction between shear and axial force, and shear and bending. When plotted in full, they demonstrate no effect of shear on axial or bending strength for values of shear less than half the representative shear strength. Further, for a level of shear equal to 70 % of representative shear strength, the reduction in axial or bending strength is less than 5 % of the corresponding representative axial or bending strength: this is the origin of the 0,7 in Formula (13.3-11).

The requirement when torsion is present to use a value of yield strength reduced to account for torsion is also based on the equivalent provision in Reference [A.13.2-22].

## A.13.3.5 Piles

No guidance is offered.

A.13.4 Tubular members subjected to combined forces with hydrostatic pressure

## A.13.4.1 General

This subclause provides both beam-column stability and strength design interaction formula for the cases in which a tubular member is subjected to axial tension or compression, and/or bending combined with external hydrostatic pressure. The design formulae are formulated so that the effects of capped-end actions can be included irrespective of whether they are calculated directly within the structural analysis or not. The purpose of providing formulae in this form is to facilitate tubular member design by the two forms of analysis commonly used by designers. In the limit when the hydrostatic pressure is zero, the design formulae in this subclause reduce to those given in 13.3.

In the formulae, hoop compression is not explicitly included in the analysis, but its effect on member design is considered within the design interaction formulae. To facilitate the application of these particular formulae, the hoop collapse design check stipulated in 13.2.6 should be satisfied first.

A structural analysis in which the capped-end axial compression is explicitly included in the analysis, is preferred, because it allows for a more precise redistribution of the capped-end forces based on the relative stiffnesses of the braces at a node.

As the redistribution of the capped-end axial compression is minimal, because of similar brace sizes at a node, the difference between including or excluding the capped-end axial compression in the analysis is usually small. Further discussion of the development of the formulae in this subclause can be found in References [A.13.4-1] and [A.13.4-2]. A collection of the test data and additional comparisons of the design formula with the test data can be found in Reference [A.13.2-1].

## A.13.4.2 Axial tension, bending and hydrostatic pressure

In the presence of tensile forces in members, external hydrostatic pressure has three main effects:

a) a reduction of the axial tension due to the presence of capped-end axial compression;   
b) a reduction of the axial tensile strength $\left( f_{ \mathrm{ t } } \right)$ caused by hoop compression, resulting in $f_{ \mathrm{ t , h } } ,$   
c) a reduction of the bending strength $\left( f_{ \mathrm{ b } } \right)$ caused by hoop compression, resulting in $f_{ \mathrm{ b , h } } .$

As demonstrated in Reference [A.13.4-2], bending hydrostatic pressure interaction is similar to axial tension hydrostatic pressure interaction. The reduced axial tensile and bending strengths, as given by Formulae (13.4-8) and (13.4-9), were derived from the following ultimate strength interaction formulae, which are doubly-modified versions of the Beltrami-Haigh yield function:

— combined axial tension and hydrostatic pressure:

$$\left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}}}\right)^{2 \eta} + 2 \nu \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}}}\right) \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}}{f_{\mathrm{y}}}\right) = 1, 0 \tag{A.13.4-1}$$

— combined bending and hydrostatic pressure:

$$\left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}}}\right)^{2 \eta} + 2 \nu \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}}{f_{\mathrm{h}}}\right) \left(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}}{f_{\mathrm{b}}}\right) = 1, 0 \tag{A.13.4-2}$$

where υ is Poisson's ratio, taken for steel as 0,3 in the derivation of Formulae (13.4-8) and (13.4-9).

The Beltrami-Haigh yield function is similar to the Mises-Hencky function in that it is elliptical, has the same tension-tension, tension-compression, etc., quadrants, but the cross-term is factored by 2υ whereas Mises-Hencky has no factoring. This factoring has the effect of shortening the major axis but lengthening the minor axis) [A.13.3-1]. The cross-term in Formula (A.13.4-1) is positive, because axial tension and external pressure generate stress in the opposite sense, i.e. tension versus compression. The same sign is adopted in Formula (A.13.4-2), which indicates it is the tensile zone of the bending stress distribution that governs ultimate strength.

To obtain the axial tensile and bending strengths from Formulae (A.13.4-1) and (A.13.4-2), the $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t } }$ and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b } }$ terms are represented by $f_{ \mathrm{ t , h } }$ and $f_{ \mathrm{ b , h } } ,$ respectively, and the positive roots taken of the resulting quadratic formulae.

In References [A.9.1-2] and [A.13.4-3], a formula identical to Formula (A.13.4-1) but without the η parameter, was adopted for the design of tubular members under combined axial tension and hydrostatic pressure. It was the first modified form of the Beltrami-Haigh formula created by replacing $f_{ \mathrm{ y } }$ by $f_{ \mathrm{ h } }$ in the hoop component: in the original form of the formula, all stress components were normalized by yield strength. This was later found to be conservative for elastic conditions, such as in the design of tendons of tension leg platforms. A further modification was made to the formula to remove this unnecessary conservatism by introducing η in Formula (A.13.4-1) [A.13.4-2]. The use of η results in a family of interaction curves representing different hoop collapse to yield strength ratios （$f_{ \mathrm{ h } } / f_{ \mathrm{ y } } )$ .

When the calculated axial tensile stress is greater than or equal to the capped-end axial compression, i.e. $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t } } > \sigma_{ \mathrm{ q } } ,$ the member is subjected to net axial tension. For this case, the member is not susceptible to local buckling.

When the calculated axial tensile stress is less than the capped-end axial compression, i.e. $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ t } } < \sigma_{ \mathrm{ q } } ,$ the member is subjected to net axial compression and to a quasi-hydrostatic pressure condition. (A member is subjected to a pure hydrostatic pressure condition when the net axial compressive stress is equal to the capped-end axial stress, i.e. $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , c } } = \sigma_{ \mathrm{ q } } . )$ Under this condition, there is no member instability. Hence, for the case of $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ { t } } } < \sigma_{ \mathrm{ { q } } } ,$ both the local strength check, Formula (13.4-13), and the elastic local buckling check, Formula (13.4-18), should be satisfied.

The test data for tubular members subjected to combined axial tension and hydrostatic pressure (no bending) were taken from Reference [A.13.2-19]. Figure A.13.4-1 presents a comparison between these data and the predictions of Formula (13.4-7) together with the statistics of the fit. Highlighted are test specimens with weld defects that could have had a detrimental effect on strength, and specimens that were not ring stiffened. These non-stiffened specimens are seen to generate relatively high bias values.

Comparison of the statistics of this fit with the corresponding ones in the first edition of this document shows that the bias has increased from 1,075 to 1,103 and the $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ increased from 0,098 to 0,112. In simple terms, the introduction of the cosine interaction compared with the linear one should have reduced the bias. However, the replacement by $f_{ \mathrm{ t , h } }$ for $f_{ \mathrm{ t } }$ in the denominator of the first term indicates bias, at least, was likely to increase in the presence of pressure, as it has done.

## A.13.4.3 Axial compression, bending and hydrostatic pressure

Capped-end axial compression arising from hydrostatic pressure does not cause column buckling. It is therefore incorrect to determine the reduced column buckling strength by subtracting the capped-end axial compression from the in-air buckling strength calculated by Formula (13.2-5) or Formula (13.2-6). An analogy to the hydrostatic pressure problem is the design of offshore platform conductors, as discussed in Reference [A.13.4-4]. Thus, for the overall stability check, Formula (13.4-14), only the calculated axial compression $\left( \sigma_{ \mathrm{ c } } \right)$ is used.

The effect of capped-end axial compression is manifested in two ways. Firstly, it leads to earlier yielding of the member in the presence of the additional external axial compression. Earlier yielding in turn results in a reduced column buckling strength, as given by Formula (13.4-15). When there is no hydrostatic pressure, i.e. $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ q } } = 0$ , Formula (13.4-15) reduces to the in-air case of Formula (13.2-5). Secondly, it contributes to the net axial compression （$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c , c } } )$ , which is used for the local strength check, Formula (13.4-13).

In addition, the elastic local buckling criterion, Formula (13.4-18), should be satisfied.

The test data for tubular members subjected to combined axial compression, bending, and hydrostatic pressure were taken from References [A.13.2-7], [A.13.2-13], [A.13.2-14] and [A.13.2-19].

The comparisons between test data and predictions using the formulae are presented Figures A.13.4-2 and A.13.4-3 for short and long columns, respectively: the statistics of the comparisons are indicated. Highlighted are specimens which were not subjected either to bending or to axial compression, as discussed in this subclause.

Further, the lower range of $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ values is dominated by non-bending cases and that all of the cases governed by Formula (13.4-13), local buckling, bending and pressure, involve no axial compression.

A comparison between the statistical characteristics of Figure A.13.4-2 and the corresponding values in the first edition of this document shows a small reduction in both bias (from 1,199 to 1,176) and VR (from 0,134 to 0,101). This is a result of:   
a) Adopting the maximum value of $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ whereas, in the first edition of this document, the maximum value was replaced by the value calculated using the hydrostatic check of Formula (13.2-24) should this exceed unity. The reason for instigating this was because, in a draft of this document, an attempt was made to anticipate and avoid software problems in trying to solve Formulae (13.4-8) and (13.4-9) for values of B, Formula (13.4-10), greater than unity, which would be the consequence of Formula (13.2-24) exceeding unity.

b) For interaction between local buckling and bending, the change from the linear form to the cosine form which was also extended to include interaction between local buckling, bending and pressure, Formula (13.4-13).

A comparison between the statistical characteristics of Figure A.13.4-3 and the corresponding values in the first edition of this document shows increases in both bias (from 1,197 to 1,326) and $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ (from 0,091 to 0,150). In addition to a) and b), this is a result of:

c) Consistent use of $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ when calculating the statistical characteristics of the relevant formulae, in particular, in Formula (13.4-14), dividing $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ in the Euler amplification terms by $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ and, in Formula (13.4-17), dividing $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ x } }$ by $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ .

d) Eliminating a possible error in the original $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ calculation.

The purpose for highlighting the specimens in Figures A.13.4-2 and A.13.4-3 that were not subjected to axial compression or bending is to provide an opportunity to further examine the impact of the cosine interaction between local buckling and bending, already considered in A.13.3.3, as well as the effect of adopting the same failure criterion for bending in the presence of pressure independent of whether the axial force is tensile or compressive, as described in A.13.4.2.

As noted in A.13.3.3, in the absence of pressure, the effect of introducing the cosine form to axial compression bending interaction was to reduce the bias, $X_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ from 1,246 to 1,096. However, when pressure is involved, Figure A.13.4-2, the reduction was only from 1,199 to 1,176. This suggests a counteracting effect that leads to an increase in bias. This is particularly obvious when only the unstiffened specimens in Figure A.13.4-2 are considered for which the bias is 1,242 and the $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ is 0,075 together with the specimens in Figure A.13.4-3 controlled by local buckling, bending and pressure for which the bias is 1,228 and the $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ is 0,027. The common factor generating these high biases is a conservative determination of $f_{ \mathrm{ b , h } }$ , the representative bending strength in the presence of external hydrostatic pressure, given by Formula (13.4-9). As noted, $f_{ \mathrm{ b , h } }$ assumes failure occurs in tension in the tension compression quadrant of the Beltrami-Haigh yield function whereas, under a combination of axial compression and bending, failure is likely to be precipitated by yield in the compression-compression quadrant.

A preliminary examination of assuming compression-compression quadrant failure for the unstiffened specimens governed by local buckling, bending and pressure in Figures A.13.4-2 and A.13.4-3 is, for Figure A.13.4-2, to reduce the bias to 1,090 while the $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ increases to 0,106, and for Figure A.13.4-3, to reduce both the bias to 0,913 and the $V_{ \mathrm{ R } }$ to 0,018. Whilst clearly the accuracy has improved, the column specimens of Figure A.13.4-3 are now non-conservatively predicted. It is concluded that, although the local buckling, bending and pressure formulation of Formula (13.4-13) could be rewritten to recognize failure occurs in the compression-compression quadrant of the Beltrami-Haigh yield function, the use of the cosine interaction between local buckling and bending when pressure is also present seems to be non-conservative and possibly should be replaced by its linear alternative, but only after further investigation.

Calculation of $X_{ \mathbf{ m } }$

For comparing design formula predictions with test data, a case of combined axial compression, bending, and hydrostatic pressure is used as an example to illustrate the procedure. In a typical test, values of axial compression, bending, external pressure and capped-end stress are measured at member failure. The test values are denoted by $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t e s t } }$ for axial compression, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t e s t } }$ for bending, $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ h , t e s t } }$ for hoop stress due to external pressure, and $\sigma_{ \mathrm{ q , t e s t } }$ for capped-end stress. All components of the test values contain bias and these biases cannot be accurately determined individually. In the comparison of the test data with the predicted values, it is assumed that the bias for all components is the same (say, $X_{ \mathrm{ b i a s } } )$ .

In the calculation of member utilization ratio using, e.g. Formulae (13.4-19) to (13.4-21), all components of measured test values are modified by dividing them by a constant parameter, $X_{ \mathrm{ m } } ,$ and the modified test values are then substituted into the formulae to determine the corresponding utilization ratio. All partial resistance factors are excluded (i.e. set to 1,0) in the calculation. An iterative procedure is necessary to determine a particular $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ value （$X_{ \mathrm{ b i a s } } )$ that yields a utilization ratio of 1,0. This value of $X_{ \mathrm{ b i a s } }$ is a measure of the accuracy of the design formula against the test data in terms of the ratio of test strength to predicted strength. Each of the Formulae (13.4-19) to (13.4-21) generates a different $X_{ \mathrm{ b i a s } } \mathrm{ . }$ the largest value governs. Depending upon the assumed $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ value, some numerical instability can occur, but this should not affect the determination of the correct $X_{ \mathrm{ b i a s } } .$

Using Test No. C3JD of the Steinmann and Vojta data [A.13.2-7] as an example, this tubular member has an outside diameter of 168,3 mm, a thickness of 3,96 mm, an overall length of 4 191 mm, Young’s modulus of 167 379 $\mathrm{ N } / \mathrm{ m m }^{ 2 }$ , and yield strength of 353,9 $\mathrm{ N } / \mathrm{ m m }^{ 2 } ,$ . At failure, the measured test components show an axial compressive stress of $149 , 2 \ \mathrm{ N / m m }^{ 2 }$ , bending stress of $174 , 1 \ \mathrm{ N / m m^{ 2 } }$ , and a hoop stress due to hydrostatic pressure of $88 , 7 ~ \mathrm{ N / m m }^{ 2 }$ . Figure A.13.4-4 shows how the calculated value of utilization ratio varies with the assumed $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ value. The calculated $X_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ that yields a utilization ratio of 1,0 is 1,832. Note that at failure for this example, the test value of hydrostatic pressure exceeds the representative strength.

A.13.5 Effective lengths and moment reduction factors

The effective length used for a bracing member in framed structures is important for determining its axial compressive strength.

Based on experience with the use of non-linear pushover analyses, it was concluded in Reference [A.13.5-1] and others that the accuracy of linear design predictions is significantly improved by using

buckling lengths determined from refined analysis. Studies indicate that buckling lengths for real, three dimensional structures demonstrate little variation when actions are increased up to collapse. Thus, buckling lengths calculated for the initial elastic loading regime are, in fact, representative throughout the complete loading history.

The effective lengths for initial conditions can be calculated for an X-frame through the use of the differential formulae given in Reference [A.13.5-2] or for a general structural component through the use of ϕ functions derived from differential formulae, see Reference [A.13.5-3]. Use of ϕ functions implies that exact solutions are obtained for the considered buckling problem. General effective buckling lengths have been derived using ϕ functions incorporating end flexibility of members. The results for an X-brace with four equal-length members are shown in Figure A.13.5-1 as a function of the force distribution in the system, expressed by the ratio Q/P (where P is the maximum compressive force in the X-brace structure), and of the non-dimensional end rotational stiffness parameter, ρ, which is defined by:

$$\rho = \frac{C L}{E I} \tag{A.13.5-1}$$

In this formula, C is the rotational stiffness at a node and I is the moment of inertia of the tubular member. C should take into account the local joint flexibility [A.13.5-4] and the flexural and torsional stiffnesses of the incoming members. L refers to centre line to centre line distances between end nodes, i.e. excluding the intermediate X-joint node.

Figures A.13.5-1 to A.13.5-3 provide effective length factors as a function of the rotational stiffness of the member ends and the ratio of the axial forces in the braces for three X-brace configurations:

a) equal segment lengths;   
b) a segment length ratio of 0,6 to $^{ 0 , 4 ; }$   
c) a segment length ratio of 0,7 to 0,3.

In developing Figures A.13.5-1 to A.13.5-3, the local bending stiffness at the X-joint is assumed to be infinite. The torsional stiffness of incoming members at the X-joint has been conservatively neglected.

Figure A.13.5-1 indicates that for realistic end conditions $\left( \rho > 3 \right)$ and for single braces, i.e. when $Q / P = 1$ (when $Q / P = 1$ , the Q-loaded member has no effect on the P-loaded member), a K factor with respect to the full X-brace length of less than 0,8 (i.e. less than 1,6 of 0,5 L) is acceptable provided end joint stiffnesses do not diminish as the braces become fully loaded. Experimental results relating to frames seem to confirm 0,7 with respect to the full brace length is acceptable, which is confirmed by the results in Figure A.13.5-1 and recommended in Table 13.5-1.

In Table 13.5-1, a K factor of 0,8 with respect to the longer segment length is recommended for X-braces in which $Q / P \leq 0$ . This value is well supported by the results in Figure A.13.5-3 for unequal X-braces with realistic end conditions $\left( \rho = 3 \ \mathrm{ t o } \ 5 \right)$ . For equal X-braces, an unusually high rotational end stiffness is required （$100 / \rho < 7 )$ to obtain a K factor of 0,8 (Figure A.13.5-1). Notwithstanding, the experimental results studied in Reference [A.13.5-5] support a K factor value of 0,8 for equal X-braces. This can be attributed to the fact that significant rotational restraint is provided at the X-joint and at member ends.

For realistic end conditions and when both X-braces are in compression, a K factor of 0,7 with respect to the full member length may be used. Implicitly, the X-joint is not braced.

Traditionally, to estimate the effective length of an unbraced column, such as topsides legs, the alignment chart in Figure A.13.5-4 has been used to provide a fairly rapid method for determining K values. This alignment chart has been used in a number of editions of AISC 360 [A.13.3-5] as well as in API RP 2A, both WSD and LRFD. Permission is given in these API documents to modify the chart to allow for conditions-`,,,` different from those assumed in the development of the chart: this same permission was given in the first ,``,, edition of this document.`, `,,

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk4_e1a7e294f140fce1f38fcdff33db6fd36b90d524056e870dc6c334b845be72d6.jpg)

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk4_81620cf63c9611429a8d7f54b14f8f4a4f828d3d62896af996524a977913d001.jpg)

![](ISO_19902_2020/chunk4_5971af67d9d60d0b050566473ff9e492a73c9b5c1175f46ec224d484a539577f.jpg)

The subscripts A and R refer to the joints at the two ends of the column section being considered. G is defined as:

$$G = \frac{\sum \frac{I_{c}}{L_{c}}}{\sum \frac{I_{0}}{L_{0}}}$$

where

Σ indicates a summation of all members rigidly connected to that joint and lying in the plane in which buckling of the column is being considered;

$I_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the moment of inertia;

$L_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ is the unsupported length of the column section;

$I_{ 0 }$ is the moment of inertia;

$L_{ 0 }$ is the unsupported length of a girder or other restraining member.

$I_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ and $I_{ 0 }$ are taken about axes perpendicular to the plane of buckling being considered.

For column ends supported by, but not rigidly connected to, a footing or foundation, G is theoretically infinity. It may be taken as 10 for practical designs unless designed as a friction free pin. If the column end is rigidly attached to a properly designed footing, G may be taken as 1,0. Smaller values may be used if justified by analysis.

Figure A.13.5-4 — Alignment chart for determining the effective length of unbraced columns

The alignment chart in Figure A.13.5-4 assumes that, in addition to the portal legs, the topsides structure above and the topmost jacket substructure below the portal legs, are all unbraced. AISC 360, for example, also provides an alignment chart for when all three bays are braced against sidesway. For many fixed offshore structures, both the topsides structure above and the topmost jacket substructure below the portal legs, are braced while the portal legs are unbraced. Ku et al. in [A.13.5-8], treated this configuration as an eigenvalue buckling problem using an advanced finite element package and found that, even for a topsides of relatively minimal structure, the effective length of the portal legs studied in their examples was always less than 1,78. This value is believed to be representative of typical portal frame columns. For use in Table 13.5-1, a slightly conservative value of 1,80 was adopted.

Ku et al. also calculated the K value in accordance with the first edition of this standard. The absence of the summation sign in the numerator of the formula for G in Figure A.13.5-4 was highlighted. The resulting K values ranged from 2,32 for the simplest topsides configuration to 1,80 for the most complex configuration, all conservative with respect to the finite element buckling solution. The omission of the summation sign in the numerator was an editing error, the summation sign should have been included as shown in the current version of Figure A.13.5-4.

Given the findings of Ku et al., it is possible that the alignment chart presented in Figure A.13.5-4 is no longer applicable in the design/assessment of typical fixed offshore structures. However, until experience is gained with the changes introduced into Table 13.5-1 and the implications of these findings have been considered further, it is not intended that Figure A.13.5-4 be deleted.

For cantilever tubular members, an independent rational analysis is required for the determination of appropriate effective length factors. Such an analysis should take full account of all large deflection (P-Δ) effects. For a cantilever tubular member, $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i } = 1 , 0$ , where $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i }$ is the moment reduction factor.

The purpose of using of $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i }$ in the interaction Formulae (13.3-3) and (13.4-14) is to obtain an equivalent moment for the moment pattern to which the beam column is subjected that more accurately reflects the effect of the moment pattern on beam-column buckling of the member. Further discussion can be found in Reference [A.13.5-6], where more accurate expressions are provided — particularly for relatively low levels of axial compression. The $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i }$ values recommended in Table 13.5-1 are similar to those recommended in Reference [A.13.5-7] and its commentary.

The radial force component per unit circumferential length at a junction (see the right hand side of Figure A.13.6-2) is proportional to the global longitudinal stress in the tubular due to factored actions and the tangent of the cone angle, i.e. radial force ∝ （$\sigma_{ \mathrm{ a , t } } + \sigma_{ \mathrm{ b , t } } ) t$ t tanα, see Figure A.13.6-2. This radial force is additional to any action effects caused by hydrostatic pressure.

The radial force results in a local bending moment and associated shear forces at the junction. The resulting local bending stresses in the tubular and the cone sides of the junction are given by Formulae (13.6-4) and (13.6-5). Both formulae are based on results presented in Reference [A.13.6-1].

## A.13.6.3 Strength requirements without external hydrostatic pressure`---

## A.13.6.3.1 General

No guidance is offered.

## A.13.6.3.2 Local buckling within conical transition

For local buckling under axial compression and bending, conical transitions with an apex angle less than $60^{ \circ }$ may be considered as equivalent cylinders with the local cone wall thickness and a diameter equal to $D_{ s } /$ cosα. For conical transitions of constant wall thickness, it is conservative to use the diameter at the larger end of the cone for $D_{ s } .$ .

Offshore structures generally have a very small number of cones. Thus, it can be expeditious to design the cones with a geometry such that the representative local buckling strength of the conical transition is equal to the yield strength, i.e. use Formula (13.2-8) given in 13.2.3.3.

## A.13.6.3.3 Junction yielding

When the hoop stress is tensile, the strength of the junction is determined by a yield check in accordance with the Mises-Hencky yield criterion.

## A.13.6.3.4 Junction buckling

The strength of the junction with regard to buckling is checked for the absolute largest value of the,,,`-- compressive hoop stress. Formula (13.6-15) is the same as Formula (A.13.4-1), apart from the addition-``,` of partial resistance factors in the former. The value suggested for the calculation of $f_{ \mathrm{ h e } }$ is based on the,,,`` results in Reference [A.13.6-1].

## A.13.6.3.5 A.13.6.3.5 Junction fatigue

The stress concentration factors are derived directly as the ratio between the maximum global plus local stresses normal to the junction and the global axial stresses in the tubular or the cone, respectively, as derived from forces due to factored actions.

## A.13.6.4 Strength requirement with external hydrostatic pressure

## A.13.6.4.1 Hoop buckling

Hoop buckling is analysed in a similar manner to that for a tubular subjected to external hydrostatic pressure, using equivalent geometry properties.

## A.13.6.4.2 Junction yielding and buckling

The action effect from external hydrostatic pressure is added directly to the other stresses at the junction when performing the utilization checks with respect to yielding and buckling.

## A.13.6.5 Ring design

No guidance is offered.

A.13.7 Dented tubular members

## A.13.7.1 General

The design recommendations are tailored to dented tubulars with dimensions and material yield strengths typical of offshore structure members （$f_{ \mathrm{ y } } \leq 500$ MPa and $D / t \leq 120 ]$ ). Because of the lack of test data for larger dent depths, the applicability of the proposed equations for dented members should be limited to $h / D \leq 0 { , } 3$ and $h / t \leq 10$ .

The most significant parameter affecting the residual strength of dented members is dent depth. Experimental and analytical data [A.13.7-1], [A.13.7-2], [A.13.7-3], [A.13.7-4] have shown that dent length and shape all have relatively negligible effects on the strength of a dented member. Furthermore, provided the dent is located length-wise in the middle half of the member, the loss of strength in a dented member seems insensitive to dent location [A.13.7-2].

The formulae in this subclause are based largely on those of Reference [A.13.7-5] although the force format adapted therein has been converted to a “stress” format for inclusion in this document.

## A.13.7.2 Dented tubular members subjected to tension, compression, bending or shear

## A.13.7.2.1 General

The tension, compression and bending recommendations contained in this subclause are based on a programme of testing carried out since the late 1970s. Hydrostatic pressure recommendations have not been included in 13.7 due to limited data. Applicable tests up to 1995 have been documented in the references cited.

## A.13.7.2.2 Axial tension

The strength formula for axial tension relies on yielding of the steel of the dented cross-section whose cross-sectional area is assumed unaltered by the damage.

## A.13.7.2.3 Axial compression

Dented tubular members subjected to axial compression fail primarily due to overall column buckling, with or without local buckling. The capacity of the dented member has been reduced by $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ with respect to the intact cross-section to account for the reduced effective cross-sectional area of the dented section.

The parameter $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ defined in Formula (13.7-14), is discussed below.

a) Column buckling

The representative axial compressive strength for members with an out-of-straightness, $\varDelta y ,$ which is not necessarily a consequence of the damage, is determined from Formulae (13.7-5) and (13.7-6), which account for the additional bending stress on the dented cross-section due to the member outof-straightness. Formula (13.7-5) deals with an out-of-straightness for dented tubulars that is still within the corresponding fabrication tolerance for intact members, i.e. 0,001 of the length. As such, only the effect of the reduction in effective cross-sectional properties at the dent should be taken into account. For an out-of-straightness greater than the fabrication tolerance, only the out-of-straightness in excess of the tolerance should be considered [Formula (13.7-6)], because the column buckling Formulae (13.2-5) and (13.2-6) already account for Δy values up to the level of the tolerance.

The column buckling formulae are similar to the intact member formulae [Formulae (13.2-5) and (13.2-6)] except that λ has been replaced by $\lambda_{ \mathrm{ d } } ,$ the column slenderness parameter that accounts for the effects of denting on cross-sectional properties. The test database was obtained from several different investigators, see References [A.13.2-6], [A.13.2-9], [A.13.7-1] to [A.13.7-4], and [A.13.7-6] to [A.13.7-13]. A comparison between the test data and the predictions using Formulae (13.7-5) and (13.7-6) is given in Figure A.13.7-1.

b) Local buckling

The local buckling formula for dented members is similar to that for intact tubular members except that the parameter $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ has been introduced [Formulae (13.7-7) and (13.7-8)] to account for the reduced strength of the dented cross-section. Discussion of the dented member parameters $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ and $\xi_{ \mathrm{ m } }$ (see A.13.7.2.4) can be found in Reference [A.13.7-14].

The results of column tests on relatively short damaged tubulars $\left( \lambda_{ \mathrm{ d } } < 0 , 252 \right)$ are plotted normalized with respect to their intact strength [Formulae (13.2-8) and (13.2-9)] against the dent damage ratio $h / t$ in Figure A.13.7-2. Also plotted is the cross-sectional area dented member parameter, $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } } ,$ [Formula (13.7-14)]. The appropriateness of $\xi_{ \mathrm{ c } }$ to represent the effects of dent damage on the local buckling strength is clearly seen.

## A.13.7.2.4 Bending

When dented tubulars are subjected to bending moments resulting in tensile (positive) or zero (neutral) stresses in the centre region of the dent, the bending strength of the dented tubular is not appreciably lower than that of an intact member. The representative bending strength formulae for members under positive [Formula (13.7-16)] or neutral [Formula (13.7-20)] bending are thus similar to that for intact members [Formula (13.2-11)].

For members subjected to bending moments resulting in compressive (negative) stress in the centre region of the dent, the bending strength of the dented member is reduced compared with that of the intact

member. Test data from References [A.13.7-9] and [A.13.7-15] indicate that the reduction in strength can be approximated by the application of Formulae (13.7-15) to (13.2-11).

A comparison between test data and the prediction of the representative bending strength formula, $\xi_{ \mathrm{ m } } \times f_{ \mathrm{ b } } ,$ , is plotted in Figure A.13.7-3. The statistics of the fit are indicated on this figure.

## A.13.7.3 Dented tubular members subjected to combined forces

## A.13.7.3.1 Axial tension and bending

The tension-bending interaction formulae for dented tubulars, Formulae (13.7-24) and (13.7-26), are similar in form to the corresponding formula for intact members, Formula (13.3-1), although, for Formula (13.7-26), a less compact format is used because of the need to cater to the differences between positive and negative bending effects. The α term in Formula (13.7-26) reflects the change in the interaction between the two orthogonal moments when a dent is present, see Reference [A.13.7-14].

Recommendations for the interaction of axial tension, bending, and hydrostatic loads have not been included due to limited test data.

## A.13.7.3.2 Axial compression and bending

The format of both the overall beam-column stability checks, Formulae (13.7-29) and (13.7-34), and the strength checks, Formulae (13.7-30) and (13.7-35), for dented tubular members subjected to combined axial compression and bending is similar to that adopted for intact tubulars in 13.3.3.

For members with different effective length factors in the negative and neutral bending directions, the Euler buckling strengths, $f_{ \mathrm{ e } }$ and $f_{ \mathrm{ e , d } } ,$ are generally different and should be taken into account in Formula (13.7-34).

The value of $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i }$ used in the stability formulae for dented tubulars has been conservatively set to 1,0, although an upper limit of 0,85 is normally recommended for end-restrained intact members in laterally braced frames typical of offshore steel structures as described in Table 13.5-1. For dented members, values of $C_{ \mathrm{ m } , i }$ smaller than 1,0 may be justified, but these should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

A comparison between test data and the combined axial compression and bending strength formulae, Formulae (13.7-29), (13.7-30), (13.7-34) and (13.7-35), is plotted in Figure A.13.7-4. The statistics of the fit are indicated in this figure.

Recommendations for the interaction of axial compression, bending, and hydrostatic loads have not been included due to limited test data.

A.13.8 Corroded tubular members

One approach to estimate the strength of an approximately uniformly corroded member is to assume a reduced thickness for the entire member. The reduced thickness should be consistent with the average material loss due to corrosion. The member with the reduced thickness can then be evaluated as an intact member. This reduced thickness approach is generally conservative, as discussed in Reference [A.13.8-1]. However, caution should be exercised with respect to fatigue.

Another common case of corroded members is the presence of severe localized corrosion in the form of patches. This form of corrosion cannot be approximated as uniform. References [A.13.7-13], [A.13.8-2] and [A.13.8-3] provide formulae to estimate the local buckling strength of these corroded members as a function of the thickness loss. No information is available on the effect of localized corrosion on overall member strength. In this case, FEA or a numerical segment approach based on empirical or analytical moment-axial force-curvature (M-P-Φ) relations can be used. For fatigue sensitive conditions, a fatigue evaluation of the corroded member should also be considered.

A.13.9 Grouted tubular members

## A.13.9.1 General

Grout filling offers benefits to intact members but offers greater benefits to members suffering limited damage following impacts from vessels or dropped objects. For intact members, greater member strength and stiffness can be achieved at the expense of weight, but without any corresponding increase in environmental actions. For damaged members, growth in dent damage is inhibited, enabling the full strength of the damaged cross-section to be achieved.

Most of the available test data relates to tubulars in which grouting has been introduced following damage, usually in the form of local dents but frequently accompanied by overall bowing. The reason for this is that the use of grouting in offshore tubulars has largely been driven by the need to strengthen/stiffen damaged members.

The formulae presented in 13.9 are only applicable to fully grouted tubular members. Based on actual experience, it can be difficult to achieve a fully grouted condition in offshore repair or strengthening operations. Consequently, some reduction in the calculated residual strength can be necessary to account for the potential incomplete grouting at the end of the grouted member. Because only limited data are available for partially grouted tubular members (especially intact ones) and because defining the extent of the grout filling of tested specimens is not precise, no design formulae for partially grouted tubular members can be given at this time. However, the strength formulae for such partially filled tubulars can be formulated by assuming that the grout does not contribute either to the axial compressive strength or to the moment capacity. This is achieved by setting the terms for the fully grouted members that relate specifically to the grout to zero, see References [A.13.9-1] and [A.13.9-2].

## A.13.9.2 Grouted tubular members subjected to tension, compression or bending

## A.13.9.2.1 General

The tension, compression and bending requirements contained in this subclause are based largely on the studies reported in References [A.13.9-1] and [A.13.9-2]. Shear and hydrostatic pressure requirements are not included because of lack of data. Applicable tests up to 1995 have been documented in the above references. Figures, showing test results supporting the requirements of 13.9, are included in the appropriate subclauses.

## A.13.9.2.2 Axial tension

The strength formula for axial tension reflects only yielding of the steel cross-section. The contribution of the grout to the tensile capacity of the fully grouted member has been conservatively ignored. When complete grouting can be demonstrated, advantage can be taken of the benefits of the grouting.

## A.13.9.2.3 Axial compression

The axial compressive strength of fully grouted tubular members is determined from Formula (13.9-8) and (13.9-9). These column buckling formulae are similar to the intact and non-grouted member strength formulae [Formulae (13.2-5) and (13.2-6)] except that the slenderness parameter λ has been replaced by $\lambda_{ \mathrm{ g } }$ and the representative local buckling strength $f_{ \mathrm{ y c } }$ has been replaced by the axial squash strength $f_{ \mathrm{ u g } }$ of the fully grouted member.

The test data for fully grouted intact tubulars are taken from References [A.13.9-1] and [A.13.9-3] to [A.13.9-5]. Similar data for fully grouted damaged tubulars are taken from References [A.13.9-3] to [A.13.9-8]. A comparison between the test data and the predictions using the strength formulae is presented in Figure A.13.9-1.

## A.13.9.2.4 Bending

The bending strength of fully grouted tubular members may be calculated from Formula (13.9-19). The bending strength of the dented section is found from a second order fit to the exact formula, simply expressed in terms of dent depth to diameter ratio. The effect of the presence of the grout is based on an approximation to the semi-graphical representation of this feature in BS 5400 [A.13.9-9].

## A.13.9.3 Grouted tubular members subjected to combined forces

## A.13.9.3.1 Axial tension and bending

For a fully grouted, intact tubular subjected to combined axial tension and bending forces, there are several ways to estimate its strength. The member may be assessed using Formula (13.3-1) by neglecting the effect of the grout or using Formula (13.9-19) if the maximum stress due to tension is small in comparison to that due to bending. For a fully grouted, dented tubular member, Formulae (13.7-24) and (13.7-26) may be used by replacing $f_{ \mathrm{ b } }$ with $f_{ \mathrm{ b , g } } .$

## A.13.9.3.2 Axial compression and bending

The design requirements are based on those given in Reference [A.13.9-9] for concrete-filled tubular members subjected to combined axial compression and bending. The background to the design requirements is documented in References [A.13.9-10] and [A.13.9-11]. The interaction formulae for fully concrete-filled tubular members are judged to be applicable to grout-filled tubular members because both their behaviour and the contribution of the grout to the strength are very similar to those of concrete-filled tubulars.

The parameter, $K_{ 1 } ,$ as given in Formulae (13.9-28) and (13.9-29), is the non-dimensional axial compressive strength of the member. A slightly different $K_{ 1 }$ formula is given in Reference [A.13.9-9]. The significance of the parameters $K_{ 2 }$ and $K_{ 3 }$ is illustrated in Figure A.13.9-2. The influence of the parameter $K_{ 2 }$ is low for tubular members having a small outer diameter and a high slenderness ratio, regardless of the $D / t$ ratio. Low values of $K_{ 2 }$ generally also mean a low value of $K_{ 3 } ,$ , which can be negative for very small diameters and a high slenderness ratio. In general, the advantageous effect of grouting resulting in increased strength diminishes as the diameter becomes smaller.

## A.14 Strength of tubular joints

A.14.1 General

The historical development of tubular joint strength provisions for offshore structures is summarized in A.14.3.

Major updates compared with the previous edition of this document are detailed in the following subclauses and involve a relaxation of the $2 / 3$ limit on tensile strength, new $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ and $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ formulations, and a change in the form of the brace load interaction formula. Further, the limit on yield strength has been increased to 800 MPa as described in A.13.1.

A.14.2 Design considerations

## A.14.2.1 Materials

All the empirical strength formulae are based on measured yield strength. Few test results have demonstrated low strength because of substandard material properties.

Updates of the tubular joint database and of design guidance were undertaken from 1994 to 1996 [A.14.2-1], [A.14.2-2]. At that time, some existing codes limited the useable value of yield strength to no more than $^{ 0 , 7 }$ or $2 / 3^{ \mathrm{ r d s } }$ of ultimate tensile strength. Analysis of the database [A.14.2-1] demonstrated that the limit on the ratio could be increased to 0,8 for joints with chord yield strength up to 800 MPa.

Figure A.14.2-1 shows a plot of the ratio of measured to predicted K-joint strength against the chord material yield-to-ultimate strength ratio based on the updated database [A.14.2-1]. In this plot, the predicted value is the representative joint strength from Clause 14 calculated using actual chord yield strength values and suitably upgraded to reflect joint mean strength. It can be seen from Figure A.14.2-1 that no effect of yield strength occurs for yield-to-tensile strength ratios up to 0,8. Similar observations have been made with respect to other joint types and design situations. Some steels exhibit adequate toughness even when the ratio exceeds 0,8. However, use of this limit is still considered appropriate, because strength formulae generally imply some degree of strain hardening. Lack of strain hardening can lead to large local strains and premature cracking.

The material property range is limited to $f_{ \mathrm{ y } } \leq 800$ MPa. Previously there had been a concern that the strength of joints with chord yield strength in excess of 500 MPa did not increase in proportion to the yield strength. The concern related to the potential that higher yield strength was obtained at the expense of lower ductility and lower strain-hardening capacity, thereby compromising the post-yield reserve strength on which the strength formulae rely. A re-evaluation of the test results reported in Reference [A.14.2-3] revealed that the strength formulae could still be used for joints with 500 MPa $< f_{ \mathrm{ y } } \leq 800$ MPa, as long as the limit on yield-to-tensile strength ratio did not exceed $^{ 0 , 8 }$ and provided adequate ductility could be demonstrated in both the heat affected zone and the base material. These test data were limited to a small number of joint types and loading modes with just 11 joints tested in total.

A JIP [A.14.2-4] investigated the static strength of high strength steel X-joints. It involved the testing of four compression joints (two with a yield strength of 355 MPa and one each with 500 MPa and 700 MPa) and three tension joints (one each with a yield strength of 355 MPa, 500 MPa and 700 MPa). The findings indicated that all joints performed satisfactorily in terms of strength and ductility. The results confirmed a yield-to-tensile strength ratio of not greater than 0,8 could be used to determine joint ultimate compressive strength, but not necessarily tensile strength because the tension joints were not subjected to a detailed assessment since cracking occurred prior to achieving ultimate strength.

Beyond 800 MPa, indicative capacity estimates can be obtained through use of a yield strength of 800 MPa or 0,8 times the tensile strength, whichever is the lesser.

## A.14.2.2 Design forces and joint flexibility

It has long been recognized that tubular joints can show significant linear elastic flexibility at locations, such as skirt pile bracing. Joint flexibility has sometimes been included in calculating fatigue life estimates. Fatigue life estimates for conductor framing connections can sometimes be substantially greater when linear elastic flexibilities are included in the analysis. Full non-linear joint forcedeformation relationships can be required for pushover analyses to determine system ultimate strength, especially where joint failures participate in the sequence leading to collapse. Such pushover analyses are common in design robustness studies as well as structural assessments of existing structures.

Reference [A.14.2-5] provides a robust set of formulae to model the linear elastic flexibility and stiffness of simple tubular joints. Although other sets of formulae are available, the formulae in [A.14.2-5] are wide-ranging, have physical meaning, compare well with hard data, and are simple to use both manually and computationally.

In Reference [A.14.2-1], additional analysis was undertaken and closed-form expressions were derived which could be used to generate joint non-linear force-deformation (P-δ or M-θ) relationships, in both loading and unloading regimes, for simple joints across a practical range of design situations and geometries. Details were presented in Reference [A.14.2-6]. Figure A.14.2-2 shows an example of a generated curve compared with a curve fitted to experimental data.

Reference [A.14.2-7] reports on a pilot study to assess the effect of hydrostatic pressure on tubular joint strength. Double T-joints (DT-joints, see 14.2.4) were considered, and the results indicate that joint strength can be reduced by up to 30 %, depending on geometry, brace force or moment and hydrostatic

pressure. No other studies on this subject have been identified. Hydrostatic pressure effects can be significant, especially for deep water structures.

## A.14.2.3 Minimum joint strength

In general, joint failure prior to a brace failure is undesirable, due to uncertainties in the failure mechanism and of the effect on the surrounding structure. The requirement for a minimum chord capacity of 50 % of incoming brace strength is intended to improve the relative reliability of joints and members, and to increase platform robustness. Furthermore, this requirement provides a safety net for unanticipated loads, such as support failure during loadout, unexpected weather conditions during launch or lifting, vessel collisions, and dropped objects. It also ensures a minimum capacity for connections of secondary members that take on primary importance in reserve strength assessments.

The more stringent requirement for a minimum chord capacity of 100 % of incoming brace strength for seismic actions is intended to ensure maximum robustness during extreme seismic events.

Non-critical joints may be excluded from the minimum capacity requirement. A joint is considered noncritical only if its failure does not:

— reduce the reserve strength of the structure for the considered design event;   
— reduce the capacity of the structure to withstand accidental actions;   
— have significant safety consequences;   
— have significant environmental consequences.

The 50 % requirement may be relaxed in certain limited instances, such as the connections of appurtenances for which failure of the connection would not lead to significant safety or environmental consequences.

## A.14.2.4 Weld strength

No guidance is offered.

## A.14.2.5 Joint classification

Some special cases of basic planar joint types have their own names. For example, a Y-joint with a brace angle of approximately 90° is called a T-joint. A double T- or DT-joint, appears to be a special case of an X-joint with braces at 90°. However, the axial forces in both braces of a DT-joint are reacted by beam shear in the chord while in an X-joint the brace axial force is transferred through the chord to the opposite side without any beam shear in the chord. A joint should be classified as a DT-joint if one brace is in tension and the other brace is in compression. Each brace is then treated separately as a T-joint.

A K-joint where one of the two braces has a brace angle of approximately 90° (see, for example, case a) in Figure 14.2-2) is sometimes referred to as an N-joint.

Joint classification is based on axial force pattern, as well as on joint configuration. The favourable strength factor $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ (see 14.3.3) for K-joints reflects reduced chord can ovalization when compared to that of Y-joints. $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ values for X-joints are typically worse than for Y-joints because X-joints have greater ovalization tendencies.

If the axial force in a given brace corresponds within ± 10 % to one of the standard joint types, it is permissible to classify the brace as totally of that joint type: no interpolation is required. However, many

joints have braces that are not clearly of one given type. Because force distributions are complex, an individual brace axial force is normally divided into portions for which the brace is treated, in turn, as a Y-joint, a K-joint or an X-joint. Figure 14.2-2 c) and h) contain braces with mixed classifications.

Several schemes for automating the classification process have evolved over the years. None is unique. In all of them, braces belonging to a particular joint type are identified and the geometrical information is catalogued. Braces lying in a common plane and on the same side of the joint are identified and the gap between them is computed. Each brace is evaluated based on its axial force for each design situation. Classification can change from one design situation to the next, and is often different for each brace at a given joint. Mixed classifications generally occur.

In a typical classification scheme, braces whose axial force component perpendicular to the chord is essentially balanced by axial forces in other braces on the same side of the chord are treated as K-joints. Figure 14.2-2 a), d), e) and g) are such cases, as are the lower braces shown in Figure 14.2-2 c) and h). A brace whose perpendicular force component is reacted by beam shear in the chord is treated as a Y-joint, as in Figure 14.2-2 b), even though its geometrical appearance suggests a K-joint. Finally, braces with ``` perpendicular forces that follow neither K-joint nor Y-joint patterns are treated as X-joints. In other `` classification schemes, the hierarchy is K- followed by X-, with T/Y- being the default.

Typically, these classification schemes do not address multiplanar connections, even though fixed steel offshore structures are generally space frames, not planar trusses. Furthermore, the schemes do not recognize that several braces in a given plane can simultaneously contribute to ovalization of the chord, for example, in launch frames and the other examples illustrated in Figure A.14.2-3. Such cases can produce a more adverse force distribution than is recognized in the classification schemes.

In cases such as those illustrated in Figure A.14.2-3, it is conservative to find the sum of the force components perpendicular to the chord and assume that the strength is the minimum of any one of the brace-chord intersections when acting as an X-joint. General collapse calculations or FEA can reduce the conservatism.

An alternative approach to joint classification is to use the ovalization parameter, α, from AWS D1.1 [A.14.2- 9]. The attraction of the α-based approach is that it does not require any decisions concerning classification. In a general sense, it encompasses the simple joint classification scheme described above and appears to be more applicable for multiplanar joints. However, limitations exist where:

a) α significantly exceeds baseline X-joint classification;   
b) the diameter ratio β is above 0,9; or   
c) a low value of α is not the result of classical K-joint action.

Further, AWS D1.1 does not properly incorporate the effect of gap nor addresses tension failures in the same manner as this document.

A JIP described in Reference [A.14.2-10] generated a considerable database of FEA results for multiplanar joints without overlapping braces and subjected to axial brace forces. Refined formulae were given for the ovalization parameter, α, which have been adopted in the AWS D1.1 approach.

Additional guidance specific to multiplanar T/Y-, K- and X-joints with axial forces can be found in Reference [A.14.2-11]. More information on multiplanar T/Y- and K-joints is available in References [A.14.2-12] to [A.14.2-14].

## A.14.2.6 Detailing practice

Consistent with recent API guidance [A.14.2-15], the can and stub length measurements do not include thickness tapers.

The minimum overlap dimension is a recommendation rather than an absolute requirement. There are many practical instances where smaller overlaps occur. These cases are fully amenable to analysis for both strength and fatigue and can be readily fabricated. However, any overlap in a joint reduces the extent to which in-service inspection can be performed.

In many instances, using the minimum chord can length provides a significant reduction in joint strength compared with that of a longer can. Formula (14.3-11) can be used to optimize the strength of the joint by providing sufficient can length.

A.14.3 Simple tubular joints

## A.14.3.1 General

## A.14.3.1.1 Parameter ranges

The requirements and recommendations contained in this document are based on interpretation of available data, both experimental and numerical. As with all empirically-based practices, the recommendations have specific validity ranges, although these cover a wide spectrum of the geometries and materials currently used in practice. However, differences in design practice and in application can lead to the selection of different acceptable data on which to base empirical formulae with the consequence that variations in various code joint strength requirements are, in part, due to differences in the databases.

Apart from the yield strength limit given in 14.2.1, the recommendations can be used for joints with geometries which fall outside the validity ranges given in 14.3.1 by taking the usable joint strength to be the lesser of the values calculated from:

— actual geometrical dimensions;

— actual geometrical dimensions together with, for those geometrical parameters where limits are exceeded, geometrical dimensions corresponding to the limiting values of the validity ranges of the relevant geometrical parameters.

## A.14.3.1.2 Historical background

## A.14.3.1.2.1 Early work

In the early 1970s, in the 3rd Edition of API RP 2A (1972), some simple recommendations for tubular joint strength were introduced based on punching shear principles. In the 4th Edition of API RP 2A (1973), these were enhanced by factors introduced to allow for the presence of forces in the chord and for the brace-to-chord diameter ratio (β). In the 9th Edition of API RP 2A (1977) modifications were introduced to account for joint type and loading configuration, i.e., T/Y, DT/X, and K.

Much work was done over the period 1977 to 1983, including large-scale tests to failure, which culminated in the 14th Edition of API RP 2A (1984) with substantial revisions to the punching shear stress formulae as well as in more realistic formulae to account for chord load effects and for the combined effect of brace axial and bending stresses. The alternative nominal load approach was also introduced: it gives equivalent results to the punching shear method [A.14.3-10].

In the 20th Edition of API RP 2A (1993), recommendations were added on load transfer through the chord.

Further data were added to the existing experimental database, often as a consequence of testing a simple joint as a reference in the course of examining a complex configuration, e.g. the database for in-plane bending doubled [A.14.3-1]. In addition, FEA studies were initiated to help improve the understanding of tubular joint behaviour [A.14.3-1].

In support of the development of the first edition of this document, a tubular joints JIP [A.14.2-1], [A.14.2-2] was undertaken over the period 1994-1996, which subsequently significantly influenced practice for simple and overlapping joints. This work, as well as further studies, notably by API/EWI and the University of Illinois [A.14.3-2], formed the basis of the tubular joint strength provisions of the 1st edition of this document.

## A.14.3.1.2.2 Database for ISO 19902:2007 tubular joints formulae

The general approach adopted in the JIP [A.14.2-1], [A.14.2-2] was:

a) collation of comprehensive databases of worldwide experimental and pertinent FEA results;   
b) validation and screening of the databases;   
c) fitting curves to the data;   
d) comparison of databases and of derived strength formulae with previous practice;   
e) selection of appropriate formulae.

Baseline screening criteria adopted in the JIP are described in A.14.3.1.2.3 to A.14.3.1.2.8.

## A.14.3.1.2.3 Data range for chord diameter

A lower limit of 100 mm was imposed because of the concern that small-scale specimens were not representative of fabricated joints found offshore from a material, weld or tolerance standpoint.

## A.14.3.1.2.4 K-joint gap

Some data only recorded eccentricity (see Figure 14.1-1) and not gap, which results in calculated gaps falling into a narrow range around zero. Consequently, using zero gap as a basis for separating overlapping from non-overlapping braces proved impractical. Accordingly, non-overlapping (gapped) joints were defined as those having at least a small finite gap and overlapping joints as those having at least a small finite overlap. Thus nominally zero gap specimens, $g_{ 0 } ,$ were defined by the following criterion:

$$- g_{0} \leq g \leq g_{0} \tag{A.14.3-1}$$

where

$$g_{0} = 7, 5 \mathrm{m m} \text{o r} 2 T, \text{w h i c e v e r i s t h e g r e a t e r};$$

$$T \quad \text{i s t h e t h i c k n e s s o f t h e c h o r d .}$$

Use of the above criterion excluded only a relatively small number of data from either the gapped joint or the overlapping joint database.

## A.14.3.1.2.5 Data range for other dimensions

No other limitations on dimensions were imposed. However, derived non-dimensional quantities were screened as follows:

a) Length/diameter ratio

Specimens having very low chord length to diameter ratios were removed as they were unduly affected by short chord effects and by end restraints, and because unusual chord stress flow patterns would exist at the joint. A limit on the ratio of 3 was initially selected.

b) Thickness ratio

Most data corresponded to joints with chord wall thickness nominally the same as or greater than that of the brace, in accordance with general offshore practice. For nominally the same chord and brace thicknesses and allowing for a ± 5 % variation of both, an upper limit of τ = 1,1 was selected.

## A.14.3.1.2.6 Data range for material properties

All specimens where the chord yield strength was not recorded were excluded from the database.

## A.14.3.1.2.7 Utilization of chord and brace

The data were segregated into two groups:

a) joints where nominal stresses in both brace and chord were below yield;   
b) joints where nominal stresses in brace or chord exceeded yield.

The first group was treated as true joint strength data with no reservation. The second group was treated as lower bounds to joint failure because, once yield occurred, joint deformation often became significant and impractical for the test rig to accommodate.

## A.14.3.1.2.8 Database summary

A total of 1 066 simple joint specimens with D greater than 100 mm were screened. Of these 653 specimens were validated and included in the database. The screened data were used to develop formulae for joint strength, using regression analysis based on minimizing percentage differences and using statistical calculations characterized by a 95 % survivability level and a 50 % confidence level. These formulations formed the basis of the joint strength provisions of ISO 19902:2007.

## A.14.3.1.2.9 Recent advances

Limitations in the above database were identified with respect to the full range of joint types, joint geometries, and brace and chord loading conditions of interest. For example, except for T-joints, test data on brace bending were relatively sparse as were tests with additional chord loads (i.e. in addition to equilibrium induced). This concern was addressed by exploiting FEA models properly validated against test results because they were recognized to provide relatively low cost solutions for extending the database (except in the case of joint tension failure because of the absence of an appropriate failure criterion). As a consequence, a comprehensive API/EWI numerical analysis study [A.14.3-2] resulted in over 1 500 validated FEA data.

The extended database was used to revise the joint strength formulations in 14.3, using regression analysis and statistical calculations similar to those used previously although, given the limitations of FEA in respect of joints failing in tension, tension capacity was still essentially based on test data. All of the work of this extended study led to the revised tubular joint strength formulae presented in API RP 2A WSD 21st Edition Supp. 2.

## A.14.3.2 Basic joint strength

## A.14.3.2.1 General

The calculation of $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ for a joint subjected to mixed mode loading is based on a weighted average of the values of $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ relevant for each loading mode. Taking Figure 14.2-1 h) as an example, the diagonal brace

has a 50 % K- and a 50 % X-joint classification. The representative joint axial strength can be calculated from:

$$P_{\mathrm{u j}} = 0, 50 P_{\mathrm{u j , K}} + 0, 50 P_{\mathrm{u j , X}} \tag{A.14.3-2}$$

where

Puj $P_{ \mathrm{ u j } }$ is the representative joint axial strength, in force units;   
$P_{ \mathrm{ u j , K } }$ is the representative joint axial strength for K-joint classification, in force units;   
$P_{ \mathrm{ u j , X } }$ is the representative joint axial strength for X-joint classification, in force units.

## A.14.3.2.2 Calibration of partial resistance factor

API RP 2A WSD $21^{ \mathbf{ s t } }$ Edition Supp. 2 describes the derivation of the safety factor incorporated therein. It exploits the enlarged database described in A.14.3.1.2.9. Because of improvements in the accuracy of the basic strength formulae that arose from the use of the enhanced database, it was possible to reduce the API RP 2A WSD $21^{ \mathbf{ s t } }$ Edition Supp. 2 safety factor without compromising safety levels with the consequence that the corresponding API RP 2A LRFD factor could be increased from 0,95 to 1,00: this is the partial resistance factor, $\gamma_{ \mathrm{ { R , j } } } ,$ adopted in 14.3.2.

## A.14.3.3 Strength factor, $\pmb{ Q_{ \mathrm{ u } } }$

In exploiting the database described in A.14.3.1.2.9, new formulae were derived which provided significant improvements in the coefficient of variation or which had a wider range of applicability. The axial load formula for overlapping K-joints is an example of the former and the out-of-plane bending formula is an example of the latter. With one exception, the new formulae are superficially very different from their predecessors. The availability of the new data has brought to light trends in the formulae with respect to the tubular joint non-dimensional geometric parameters not previously appreciated. These trends and their effects on the formulae are fully discussed in Reference [A.14.2-15], except for the case of X-joints in tension.

The $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ formulae for tension loaded T/Y- and DT/X-joints were derived on the basis of forces at which cracking was observed in tests. However, tension loaded joints made of thin or extremely tough steel can sustain further loading beyond first crack. Because an estimate of this reserve strength can be important in predominantly statically loaded joints, characteristic ultimate tensile strength formulae were developed [A.14.2-1] and are as follows:

a) For T/Y-joints (bias = 1,805, VR = 0,263):

$$Q_{\mathrm{u}} = 42 \beta - 4, 1 \quad \text{f o r} \beta \geq 0, 35 \tag{A.14.3-3}$$

b) For DT/X-joints (bias = 1,138, VR = 0,071):

$$Q_{\mathrm{u}} = 41 \beta - 1, 9 \quad \text{f o r} \beta \leq 0, 9 \tag{A.14.3-4}$$

$$Q_{\mathrm{u}} = 35 + (\beta - 0, 9) (32 \gamma - 285) \quad \text{f o r} \beta > 0, 9 [ \text{n o t v a l i d f o r} e / D > 0, 2 ] \tag{A.14.3-5}$$

NOTE 1 Bias is defined as the ratio of measured (test or numerical) strength to strength predicted using the recommended formulae and measured yield strength but assuming all partial factors to have a value of unity.

NOTE 2 e is the eccentricity of the two braces; see Figure 14.1-1.

The large increase in strength indicated in the second formula for DT/X-joints at high β relies on membrane stresses in the chord saddle region as the load is essentially transferred directly from one brace to the other. However, if there is any significant misalignment of the braces （$\mathrm{ i } . \mathrm{ e } . , e / D > 0 , 2 )$ , force transfer by membrane action is limited and the Formula (A.14.3-4) should be adopted over the full range of ${ \mathrm{ ~ ~ } } \beta .$

In situations where fatigue cracking is evident, the strength formulations for tension loaded $\mathrm{ T / Y } \mathrm{ - }$ and DT/X-joints based on forces at which cracking has been observed can be used to estimate the strength of the cracked joint; see Table 14.3-1. This applies for conditions in which the percentage of cracked area is not greater than 20 % of the full area. For other conditions, reference to further work [A.14.8-1], [A.14.8-2] should be made to determine the strength of the joint (also see Reference [A.14.5-5]).

Reference [A.14.3-11] introduced new strength formulations for X-joints in tension, which were adopted in NORSOK N-004 [A.14.3-12]. In addition to the characteristic capacity formula for $Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ provided in Table 14.3-1, Reference [A.14.3-11] also reported the mean capacity for X-joints under tension as given in Formula (A.14.3-6)

$$Q_{\mathrm{u}} = 9. 0 \gamma^{0. 6 \beta^{2}} \tag{A.14.3-6}$$

This formula can be used in the assessment of existing structures (see ISO 19901-9) in agreement with the regulator, where one exists.

## A.14.3.4 Chord force factor, $\pmb{ Q_{ \mathrm{ f } } }$

Compared to ISO 19902:2007, a substantial change to the chord force factor $\left( Q_{ \mathrm{ f } } \right)$ has been introduced.

a) The factor $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ given in Formula (14.3-9) includes linear terms in the nominal chord axial load and inplane bending moments, in addition to the quadratic terms retained in the parameter A, see Formula (14.3-10). This is similar in form to the chord stress function proposed in Reference [A.14.3-13] and adopted in the CIDECT design guide [A.14.2-11].   
b) Formula (14.3-9) applies over the full range of chord loads.

The $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factor adopted herein is similar to that provided in API RP 2A 22nd Edition for X-joints with the brace in compression. For X-joints with the brace in tension, modified values for the $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factor are recommended. The API RP 2A 22nd Edition formulae are based on tests and analyses with the brace in compression only. In the most recent update to NORSOK N-004 Rev 3 [A.14.3-12], it was assumed that the influence of chord loading on joint strength could be different from that when the brace is in tension. As test and analytical results were not available, the recommended $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factors for when the brace was in tension were adopted in NORSOK N-004 Rev 3 based on the following assumptions, see also Figure A.14.3-1:

— For $\beta = 1 , 0$ , the $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factor for when the brace is in tension, is assumed to mirror the case of when the brace is in compression.   
— For $\beta < 0 , 9$ , it is assumed that when the brace is in tension and the chord in compression, the $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factor mirrors the case for the brace in compression and the chord in tension. For the case with the brace in tension and the chord in tension, the $Q_{ \mathrm{ f } }$ factor is assumed to mirror the case with the brace in compression and the chord in compression.

A recent study into the validity of these assumptions [A.14.3-14] concluded that for of X-joints with $\beta > 0 , 9$ and the brace in tension, the assumption in NORSOK N-004 was sound and provided a significant

improvement in the accuracy of the strength formulation. When $\beta < 0 , 9$ , it was observed that the existing API RP 2A WSD formula better represented joint capacity for X-joints with the brace in tension. Figures A.14.3-1 (a) and A.14.3-1 (b) show the results of the FEA used to validate the assumptions in NORSOK N-004 for $\beta = 1 , 0$ and $\beta < 0 , 9$ , respectively.

## A.14.3.5 Effect of chord can length on joint strength

The reduced strength for simple Y- and X-joints with axial forces and short can lengths is supported by numerical and experimental data, see Reference [A.14.2-1].

No reduction in strength is required for K-joints with axial forces.

No guidance is provided on length effects for joints subjected to moments or for complex joints.

## A.14.3.6 Strength check

No guidance is offered.

A.14.4 Overlapping joints

The guidance in this document is primarily based on the results in Reference [A.14.2-1]. A critical assessment of design practice up to 1995 can be found in Reference [A.14.4-4]. More recent guidance can be found in Reference [A.14.4-7].

The current guidance generally avoids the need for numerical analysis in all but the most unusual or failure-critical cases. It addresses both in-plane and out-of-plane force situations, as well as out-of-plane overlap situations, which are not uncommon in offshore structures.

Generally, there is no need to calculate weld lengths. For more precise analyses, such lengths can still be necessary. Reference [A.14.4-5] reproduces formulae for these calculations.

A.14.5 Grouted joints

Grouted joints are becoming more common in new steel frame structures and joint grouting is generally a cost-effective means of strengthening older structures. Current guidance [A.14.5-1] is based upon engineering approximations and some experimental evidence, see References [A.14.5-2] to [A.14.5-6]. The experimental evidence is primarily for double-skin joints subjected to axial brace forces. Reference A.14.5-7 provides additional data for fully grouted joints, especially those subjected to brace bending moments.

$Q_{ \mathrm{ u } }$ values for Y-, X- and K-grouted joints, given in References A.14.5-1 and A.14.5-3, are reproduced in Table A.14.5-1.
